units.la: Magnifici pompam Propy'æi magna postulant ædificia, ( certè quidem haud respuunt ,) quam tamen humilis casa erubescit verecundia. Non est igitur hic permultis præfandum. Do tantum Lectori benevolo (quem ἀδεσπότῳ huic scriptiunculæ & Patronum ambio) suscepti opusculi consilium.
units.tr: Great buildings demand the grand pomp of a propylaeum (they certainly do not refuse it), though a humble cottage blushes at its own modesty. There is therefore no need for many prefatory words here. I only offer the kindly reader, whom I court as patron of this unclaimed little writing [ἀδέσποτον], the purpose of the work I have undertaken.

units.la: Nimirum ei quærere in proclivi fore suspicor, cur tot inter Christianæ Religionis Systematum examina (quà domestica, quà peregrina) in ore, oculisque omnium, cum debitâ laude volitantia, nostrum quoque se ingerat ENCHIRIDION. Rem totam paucis habeto. Ex ista scilicet, quas modo diximus, fœcunda hujusmodi lucubrationum familia, cum aliæ ant prolixitate suâ, aut ingratis fortasse minutiloquiis & subtilitatibus Juventuti, aliæ autem aliunde minus nobis placerent, visum est istis omnibus, (quâ quidem pro modu'o nostro liceret,) ire obviam incommodis: quod in hac Enchiridio præstitum esse, non sum usque adeo Suffenus, ut somniem; præstare tantum volui; de eventu, æquum est ut ipse, Lector Cordate, pro Candore tuo sententiam feras. Certè hic pluribus prodesse, Neophytos potissimum loquor, & in re Theologica minùs exercitatos, in animo cum primis habuisse, testes appello mille, Conscientiam scilicet, & plusquam mille, Cordium Scrutatorem, Deum.
units.tr: Surely he will think it an easy question why, among so many examinations of the systems of the Christian religion, some domestic and some foreign, flitting about with due praise on everyone's lips and in their eyes, our own ENCHIRIDION also thrusts itself forward. Take the whole matter in a few words. Out of that fruitful family of such labours which I have just mentioned, some were too long, others perhaps too full of thankless trifling and subtleties for young people, and others were otherwise less to my liking. It seemed good to meet all these faults, so far as my own measure allowed, in this Enchiridion. That I have achieved this I am not so much a Suffenus as to dream; I wished only to attempt it. As to the outcome, it is right that you yourself, kind Reader, pass judgment in your candour. Certainly I call to witness a thousand consciences, namely conscience, and more than a thousand, God, the searcher of hearts, that I had in mind above all to be of use to many, speaking chiefly to neophytes and to those less trained in theological matters.

units.la: Ad veritatis autem vitaeque cœlestis compendium (quo Homini Christiano antiquius nihil esse par est) tenellos & rudiores adhuc circa Religionem animos, tum stabiles, neque tardos insuper effingere, quanti interfit, nemo non videt. Viderunt utique primi illi Religionis Reformatæ præclari Pugiles, quibus erat cum hoste callidissimo, frontisque omnium in Temio durissimæ, (quamvis & eodem ignavissimo) præliandum. Viderunt ipsi tandem Papicolæ, quos Adversæ partis virtutem si laudare vetabat livor, æmulari monuit versutia: iisdem scilicet ipsi vestigiis in via sua errorum Lata consultò insistebant, quibus in Angustiore veritatis præibant Reformati. Hinc illorum quoque tot indies (hoc maximè φιλοσοφιαν seculo) blandiloquentiæ Popularis & Sophisticæ gramine obtecti Religionem à Calcaneo impetunt Anguiculi Chartacei. Cui faxit Deus ut minus in posterum indormiscamus malo; Ei certè ut apud studiosam Juventutem aliquatenus occurreret hoc Enchiridion, operam navavi.
units.tr: That it matters greatly how tender and still rough minds in religion, yet steady and not slow, are shaped to a summary of the truth and of the heavenly life (than which nothing should be dearer to a Christian man) is something no one fails to see. The first famous champions of the Reformed religion saw it, who had to fight with a most crafty enemy whose brow was of the hardest, though also most cowardly. The Papists themselves at last saw it, whom envy forbade to praise the valour of the opposing side, but cunning urged them to imitate it. They deliberately trod the same footsteps along the broad way of error as the Reformed had gone before on the narrow way of truth. Hence also, every day now (in this most philosophical [φιλοσοφίαν] age), those little paper serpents, hidden under the grass of a popular and sophistical smooth-tongued eloquence, attack religion from the heel. May God grant that we slumber less in future against this evil. For my part, I have laboured that this Enchiridion should in some measure meet them among studious youth.

Scripturæ appellandis neque credulam neque perfunctoriam ( pro modici ratione ocii ) adhibuisse operam, & 2° Ecclesiæ nostræ hic illic accomodata suffragia ( ne ista quoque Juventutem ingenuam lateant ) siqua in Libell: Corpore haud occurrunt, cum Elencho Capitum ad sinem rejecisse.

units.la: PRÆCIPUORUM THEOLOGIÆ CAPITUM
units.tr: THE CHIEF HEADS OF THEOLOGY

units.la: Tractatio brevis, per modum Dialogi.
units.tr: A brief treatment, in the manner of a dialogue.

units.la: A. Quid est Religio?
units.tr: A. What is religion?

units.la: B. Est vis illa creaturæ rationali, divinitus impressa, quâ tenetur obstricta ad cultum & obsequium Dei.
units.tr: B. It is that power, divinely implanted in the rational creature, by which it is bound to the worship and obedience of God.

units.la: A. Quanam est regula (sive norma) cultus Veri & Christiani?
units.tr: A. What is the rule (or norm) of true and Christian worship?

units.la: B. Voluntas unius Dei. Deut. 12. 32. Mat. 15. 9.
units.tr: B. The will of the one God. Deut. 12. 32. Matt. 15. 9.

units.la: A. Unde autem ista hominibus innotescit voluntas?
units.tr: A. But how is that will made known to men?

units.la: B. Ante legem à Mose traditam (quin & sub lege) multiformiter, in sacris vero Scripturis
units.tr: B. Before the law was delivered by Moses (and also under the law) in many forms, but most fully revealed afterwards in the holy Scriptures.

units.la: a Ro. 1. 19. b Ro. 1.21. turis plenissimè postmodum patefacta.
units.tr: a Rom. 1. 19. b Rom. 1. 21. ...most fully revealed afterwards in the Scriptures.

units.la: A. Voluntatem suam hominibus revelatam cur scriptis consignari voluit Deus ?
units.tr: A. Why did God wish his revealed will to be committed to writing for men?

units.la: B. Ob majorem fidei certitudinem, quæ aliàs, humana partim infirmitate, partim malitia, astúque Satanæ, decursu temporum facilius corrumperetur.
units.tr: B. For greater certainty of faith, which otherwise, partly through human weakness, partly through malice and the cunning of Satan, would more easily be corrupted as time went on.

units.la: A. Ad normam religionis constituendam (quam Scripturam esse dixisti) quæ potissimum requiruntur ?
units.tr: A. What is chiefly required for establishing the rule of religion (which you said is Scripture)?

units.la: B. Tria, Authoritas, Perfectio, & Perspicuitas.
units.tr: B. Three things: Authority, Perfection, and Perspicuity.

units.la: A. Qualis autem est Scriptura S. Authoritas ?
units.tr: A. But what is the nature of the authority of Holy Scripture?

units.la: B. Plane divina, cum sit abipso Deo aut edita, aut inspirata.
units.tr: B. Plainly divine, since it has been either issued or inspired by God himself.

units.la: A. Quid autem inde consequetur?
units.tr: A. What follows from this?

units.la: B. Authoritatem istam esse cum infallibilem, cum irrefragabilem.
units.tr: B. That this authority is both infallible and irrefutable.

units.la: A. At seposito ipsius Scriptura de se testimonio, poteritne palam fieri eam illi authoritatem deberi tanquam verbo Divino ?
units.tr: A. But setting aside Scripture's own testimony about itself, can it be shown plainly that this authority is due to it as the divine Word?

units.la: B. Potest, hominibus saltem cordatis, & veri amantibus.
units.tr: B. It can, at least for men who are sensible and lovers of truth.

units.la: A. Unde vero ?
units.tr: A. But how?

units.la: B. Aut quæris de causa efficiente primaria, aut de causis ministerialibus, intermediis, & (quæ vulgo appellantur) motivis. A. Cedo
units.tr: B. You ask either about the primary efficient cause, or about the ministerial, intermediate causes, which are commonly called motives. A. Pray go on.

units.la: A. Cedò causam Principem.
units.tr: A. Tell me the principal cause.

units.la: B. Ea alia esse non potest, quàm a Spiritus ille veritatis, qui ejusmodi (ut lubet) b omnia operatur in omnibus. a Joh. 16. 13. b 1 Cor. 12. 6. ad 10.
units.tr: B. It can be none other than that Spirit of truth who "worketh all things in all" (1 Cor. 12. 6 ff.). John 16. 13. 1 Cor. 12. 6 ff.

units.la: A. Quænam sunt causæ istæ (quas modò vocafti) intermediæ?
units.tr: A. What are those intermediate causes you just mentioned?

units.la: B. Duûm sunt genera; aliæ internæ, ex ipsa scilicet Scripturarum divina indole, proprietatibus & effectis desumptæ, aliæ autem extrinsecus accersitæ.
units.tr: B. They are of two kinds: some internal, drawn from the divine character of the Scriptures themselves, their properties and effects; others brought in from outside.

units.la: A. Da causas istius assensus internas.
units.tr: A. Give me the internal causes of this assent.

units.la: B. Sunt istæ materia (a pietatem omne genus & bonos mores ubique redolens) sensuum, in stylo etiam (ubi is occurrit) humiliore b majestas, & humano major ingenio c profunditas, d Prophetiarum de rebus maximis adimpleta veritas, e vis illa ineluctabilis & plane divina f infidelium quoque cordibus, nedum g Credentibus, multiformiter impressa, & fiqua denique sint istis similia. a Pf. 19. 8, 9, & Pf. 119. passim. b 1 Cor. 2. 4. c
units.tr: B. They are: the matter, which everywhere breathes piety of every kind and good morals; the senses, and in the style too (where it occurs), a majesty that is humble, and a depth greater than human genius; the truth of the prophecies fulfilled concerning the greatest matters; that irresistible and plainly divine power which is impressed in many ways even on the hearts of unbelievers, not to mention believers; and whatever else of this kind there may be. Ps. 19. 8, 9, and Ps. 119 passim. 1 Cor. 2. 4.

units.la: A. Da causas externas.
units.tr: A. Give the external causes.

units.la: B. Sunt istæ etiam multimodæ 1. ipsorum Amanuensium θεοπνευστων de Scriptura (præsertim Evangelica a) idque tot & tantis miraculis firmatum testimonium, de quo nulla potest apud æquos rerum æstimatores oboriri suspicio. 2. Constans & perpetua Ecclesiæ Traditio, eaq; tot suorum tantisque periculis, imò & frequentibus martyriis pro‑ pugnata. 3. Conatus inimicorum Diabolici ad Scrip. penitus delendam irriti. 4. Judæorum Evangeliohoftium infenfiffimorum suffragia veteri Testamento exhibita, cum quo Novum in subftantialibus omnino congruit.
units.tr: B. These too are of many kinds: 1. the testimony concerning Scripture (especially the Gospel) of the very writers, who were theopneustoi [θεοπνευστων], and this confirmed by so many and such great miracles that no suspicion of it can arise among fair judges of things. 2. The constant and perpetual tradition of the Church, which has been defended through so many and such great dangers, and indeed through frequent martyrdoms. 3. The attempts of the enemies of the devil to destroy Scripture utterly, which have come to nothing. 4. The support given to the Old Testament by the Jews, the most bitter enemies of the Gospel, with which the New Testament agrees entirely in its substance.

units.la: A. Annon ergo pendet Sacrorum codicum Authoritas ex testimonio Ecclesia?
units.tr: A. Then does the authority of the sacred books not depend on the testimony of the Church?

units.la: B. Nequaquam. Nam primò sequeretur inde, authoritatem Scrip. non esse divinam, sed humanam, & consequenter incertam & fallibilem, (quod Atheismum sapit,) cum hoc dato non effet verbum Dei, sed verbum hominis.
units.tr: B. By no means. For first it would follow from this that the authority of Scripture is not divine but human, and consequently uncertain and fallible (which savours of atheism), since on this supposition it would "not be the word of God, but the word of man."

units.la: A. Da alteram, si habes, rationem.
units.tr: A. Give me the other reason, if you have one.

units.la: B. Illa fumi potest ex absurdo: Nam Ecclesiæ in confesso nulla sunt omnino indicia, nedum Authoritas, nisi Scripturæ sacræ in solidum nixa; proinde hæc ab illis pendet, non vice versa.
units.tr: B. It can be drawn from the absurd consequence: for the Church, as is agreed, has absolutely no grounds, let alone authority, except as resting entirely on holy Scripture; therefore the Church depends on Scripture, not the reverse.

units.la: A. Quænam ergo partes tribuendæ sunt in hoc negotio Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: A. What part, then, is to be assigned to the Church in this matter?

units.la: B. Testimonium præbere verum Scripturis, easque populis suis, ut omni acceptatione dignas commendare, quo maxime sensu hoc elogio ornatur Ecclesia, quod sit columna & firmamentum veritatis.
units.tr: B. To bear witness to the Scriptures as true, and to commend them to its people as worthy of all acceptance; and it is in this sense above all that the Church is honoured with the description that it is "the pillar and ground of the truth."

units.la: A. De Authoritate in præsentia satis; unde constat S. Scripturam esse normam religionis persectam?
units.tr: A. Enough about authority for now; how is it established that Holy Scripture is the perfect norm of religion?

units.la: B. Id de se multis in locis ipsa testatur, nec potest illius testimonium vanitatis insimulari, fi (quod utcunque evicimus) fit divinum. 2 Tim. 3. 16, 17.
units.tr: B. Scripture itself testifies to this about itself in many places, and its testimony cannot be charged with vanity, if (as we have somehow shown) it is divine. 2 Tim. 3. 16, 17.

units.la: A. Ad quænam fe diffundit ista Script.perfeētio ?
units.tr: A. To what persons, matters, and circumstances does this perfection of Scripture extend?

units.la: B. Ad omnes personas, casus, & tempora.
units.tr: B. To all persons, cases, and times.

units.la: A. An itaque omnes possunt intelligere Scripturas ?
units.tr: A. Can everyone, then, understand the Scriptures?

units.la: B. Omnes, quantum ad eorum salutem sufficit, modo usum habeant rationis, & intelligentiam à Spiritu Sancto, mediis (ut plurimum) ordinariis,illustratam. a Jo. 20. 31. b 1 Cor. 2. 10. 1 Joh. 5. 20. Pf. 119. 18.
units.tr: B. Everyone, so far as is sufficient for their salvation, provided they have the use of reason and an understanding illuminated by the Holy Spirit, usually through the ordinary means. John 20. 31. 1 Cor. 2. 10. 1 John 5. 20. Ps. 119. 18.

units.la: A. Unde constabit Script. S. esse perspicuam ?
units.tr: A. How will it be established that Holy Scripture is perspicuous?

units.la: B. Ex æquitate Divina, quæ neminem finit in rebus tanti momenti obscuro & incerto duce uti, quin & ex compluribus ipsius Scrip. de se testimoniis. a Mic. 6. 8. 1 Cor. 14. 8. b Pf. 119, 105. Pro. 8. 9.
units.tr: B. From the divine equity, which does not allow anyone to use a dark and uncertain guide in matters of such great moment; and also from several testimonies of Scripture concerning itself. Mic. 6. 8. 1 Cor. 14. 8. Ps. 119. 105. Prov. 8. 9.

units.la: A. At multa sunt in Scripturis (earum quoque rerum quarum fides est necessaria ad salutem) profunditates & mysteria.
units.tr: A. But there are many depths and mysteries in the Scriptures, even in those matters whose belief is necessary for salvation.

units.la: B. Sunt quidem, sed homini a naturali, non b spirituali, nisi quoad modum, magnitudinem, & alias fortasse circumstantias, non quoad d rem ipsam, sive rerum credendarum substantiam; hæc enim credentibus (quantum certe ad ipsorum salutem sufficit) per verbum & Spiritum satis retegitur. a 1 Cor. 8. 14. b v. 10, & 15. c Ro. 11. 33. d Ro. 4. 18.
units.tr: B. There are indeed, but for the natural man, not the spiritual one, except as to the manner, the greatness, and perhaps other circumstances; not as to the thing itself, or the substance of the things to be believed. For these are sufficiently revealed to believers (at least as far as their salvation requires) through the Word and the Spirit. 1 Cor. 8. 14. Ibid. v. 10 and 15. Rom. 11. 33. Rom. 4. 18.

units.la: A. Quomodo dividitur Scriptura ?
units.tr: A. How is Scripture divided?

units.la: B. In eam quæ est Veteris, & quæ Novi Te& shy;stamenti.
units.tr: B. Into that of the Old and that of the New Testament.

units.la: A. Quid de libris illis censendum est, qui vulgò Apocryphi dicuntur?
units.tr: A. What is to be thought of those books commonly called Apocrypha?

units.la: B. Non sunt pro fidei regula amplexandi, quanquam illorum aliquot morum præcepta minimè aspernanda contineant.
units.tr: B. They are not to be embraced as a rule of faith, although some of them contain precepts of morals that are by no means to be despised.

units.la: A. Cur autem à Canone (sive regula fidei) exterminantur?
units.tr: A. But why are they excluded from the canon (or rule of faith)?

units.la: B. 1. Quod nunquam pro θεόπνευστοι sint à Judæis agniti, quibus concredita sunt eloquia Dei, Ro. 3. 2. 2. Quod lingua Ecclesiæ Judaicæ ignota (Græca scil.) maximam partem confcripti sunt, idque cum nulla præter Judaicam esset in terris Ecclesia visibilis. 3. Ob nonnulla à veritate & Spiritu Dei aliena in istis tradita. Cujusmodi sunt mendacium Angeli, Tob. 5. 4. 12. incantatio magica ab eodem præscripta, c. 6. 15, 16, 17. mendacium Authoris libri Sap. qui Solomonem se falsò præfert, c. 19. 7, 8. verba Macchab. 1. 2. c. 15. 38, 39. a Spiritu Dei alienissima, Judithæ 9. v. 2, 4, 10. & non pauca id genus alia.
units.tr: B. 1. Because they were never acknowledged by the Jews, to whom "the oracles of God were committed" (Rom. 3. 2), as theopneustoi [θεόπνευστοι]. 2. Because most of them were written in a language unknown to the Jewish Church (namely Greek), although there was no visible Church on earth besides the Jewish one. 3. On account of some things delivered in them that are alien to the truth and the Spirit of God. Such are the lie of the Angel (Tob. 5. 4, 12); the magical incantation prescribed by the same (ch. 6. 15, 16, 17); the lie of the author of the book of Wisdom, who falsely presents himself as Solomon (ch. 19. 7, 8); the words of Maccabees (1 Macc. 2; ch. 15. 38, 39), most alien to the Spirit of God; Judith 9. vv. 2, 4, 10; and not a few other things of this kind.

units.la: Cap. 2. De Natura Dei.
units.tr: Chapter 2. On the Nature of God.

units.la: A. VNde constat esse Deum?
units.tr: A. How do we know that God exists?

units.la: B. Non modò ex Scripturis, verum etiam ex lumine rationis naturali, ex omnium gentium testimonio, atque adeo ipsis operibus Divinis. Ro. 14. 15. b Jer. 2. 11. c Ro. 1. 19, 20.
units.tr: B. Not only from the Scriptures, but also from the natural light of reason, from the testimony of all nations, and indeed from the divine works themselves. Ro. 14. 15. b Jer. 2. 11. c Ro. 1. 19, 20.

units.la: A. Quid est Deus?
units.tr: A. What is God?

units.la: B. Est Spiritus æternus, incomprehensibilis, immutabilis, per se independenter existens, sibi soli sufficiens, in sæcula benedictus. a Joh. 4. 24. b Psal. 90. 2. c Job. 37. 19; &c. 26. 14. Ro. 11. 33. d Ex. 3. 14. Ja. 1. 17. e Is. 44. 6. Ex. 3. 14. f Gen. 17. 1. Ro. 11. 35. Job. 22. 2. &c. 35. 6, 7, 8. g Ro. 9. 5.
units.tr: B. He is an eternal, incomprehensible, immutable Spirit, existing independently through himself, sufficient to himself alone, blessed for ever. a Joh. 4. 24. b Psal. 90. 2. c Job. 37. 19; &c. 26. 14. Ro. 11. 33. d Ex. 3. 14. Ja. 1. 17. e Is. 44. 6. Ex. 3. 14. f Gen. 17. 1. Ro. 11. 35. Job. 22. 2. &c. 35. 6, 7, 8. g Ro. 9. 5.

units.la: A. Si Deus sit spiritus, cur membra ei corporea, aures, oculos, &c. passim tribuit Scriptura?
units.tr: A. If God is spirit, why does Scripture everywhere ascribe to him bodily members, ears, eyes, and so on?

units.la: B. Hoc facit non sensu proprio, sed tantum analogico, idque intellectus humani, ad naturam divinam cæcutientis, sublevandi gratia. Nam quicquid istorum membrorum subsidio rite operatur homo, id potest omne (modo & gradu infinities eminentiore) per suam essentiam simplicissimam operari Deus.
units.tr: B. It does this not in the proper sense, but only analogically, and in order to help the human understanding, which is groping about regarding the divine nature. For whatever a man rightly accomplishes with the help of these members, God can accomplish entirely through his most simple essence, in a manner and degree infinitely more eminent.

units.la: A. Si sit immutabilis, cur 1° ei tribuuntur afsectus, sive motiones humanæ? Cur 2° diserte, nec uno in loco, pœnituisse dicitur?
units.tr: A. If he is immutable, why are human affections or motions ascribed to him? And why, secondly, is it said expressly, and in more than one place, that he repented?

units.la: B. Ad horum utrumque quæsitum quod modo diximus de membris corporeis accommodari potest: ejusmodi scil. affectus Deo minime {a}convenire sensu proprio, & literali, sed figurato tantum & analogico.
units.tr: B. The answer to both of these questions can be given as we just said about the bodily members: such affections do not belong to God in the proper and literal sense, but only in a figurative and analogical sense.

units.la: A. Quomodo igitur?
units.tr: A. How then?

units.la: B. Hoc modo; Deus non amat, aut odit, dolet, aut gaudet, per ullam talem motionem, qualem in nobis cotidiè experimur homines, sed voluntas ejus (ceu effentia) simpliciffima ratione effecti ad creaturam relati, has vel illas inducit assectuum appellationes, quas ἀνθρωπομόρφως efferri vulgo dicunt Theologi.
units.tr: B. In this way: God does not love, hate, grieve or rejoice through any such motion as we human beings daily experience in ourselves. Rather, his will (like his essence, most simple) by reason of the effect related to the creature brings in these or those names of affections, which theologians commonly say are expressed anthropomorphically.

units.la: A. Nunquam ergo Deus mutat propositum suum?
units.tr: A. So God never changes his purpose?

units.la: B. Nunquam. Nam hoc aut impotentiam aut inscitiam argueret, quorum utrumvis Deo adscribere summae esset blasphemiae. Num. 23. 19. Isf. 46. 10
units.tr: B. Never. For this would argue either impotence or ignorance, and to ascribe either to God would be the greatest blasphemy. Num. 23. 19. Isa. 46. 10

units.la: A. At poenas comminatas non infligere (ut in casu Ninevitarum) mutationem aliquam voluntatis sapit?
units.tr: A. But does not failing to inflict threatened punishment (as in the case of the Ninevites) smack of some change of will?

units.la: B. In Deo nullam, quia comminationes istae sunt tantum conditionales, quae mutato in melius peccatore, non ponunt poenam, idque secundum voluntatem Dei immutabilem. Jer. 18. 7, 8, 9, 10.
units.tr: B. Not in God, because those threats are only conditional: when the sinner changes for the better, they do not impose the punishment, and this accords with the immutable will of God. Jer. 18. 7, 8, 9, 10.

units.la: A. Da alios characteres (ceu proprietates) divinae naturae in S. Scrip. traditos.
units.tr: A. Give other characters (or properties) of the divine nature handed down in Holy Scripture.

units.la: B. Ex iis sunt immensitas (ceu ) sanctitas, bonitas, justitia infinita, omniscientia, omnipotentia. Jer. 23. 24. Psal. 139. 7, 8, 9, 10. Isai. 6. 3. & c. 57. 15. Ex. 34. 6. Psal. 97. 2. Psal. 139. 2, 3, 4. Heb. 4, 13. Gen. 18. 14. Mar. 14. 36.
units.tr: B. Among them are immensity, holiness, goodness, infinite justice, omniscience, omnipotence. Jer. 23. 24. Psal. 139. 7, 8, 9, 10. Isai. 6. 3. & c. 57. 15. Ex. 34. 6. Psal. 97. 2. Psal. 139. 2, 3, 4. Heb. 4, 13. Gen. 18. 14. Mar. 14. 36.

units.la: A. Cum immensitate Dei quomodo conciliande sunt sunt ista Scripturæ, quæ Deum de loco in locum migrare statuunt, easque quæ sedem ei propriam tribunt in cœlis?
units.tr: A. How are these passages of Scripture to be reconciled with the immensity of God, which state that God migrates from place to place, and those which assign him a proper seat in the heavens?

units.la: B. Non potest vere mutare locum, qui omnem replet, Jer. 23. 24. sed ista omnia καθ' αὐτοπάθειαν intelligenda. Dicitur autem esse in cœlo, non definitive, quasi alibi eodem tempore non esset, sed manifestative, idque non simpliciter, sed tantum quoad eminentiam, quod inde scil. ibique majestatis & gloriæ sui radii potissimum eniteant. Isa. 66. 1. Psal. 19. 1. &c.
units.tr: B. He who fills all things cannot truly change place (Jer. 23. 24), but all these things must be understood as they affect us [καθ' αὐτοπάθειαν]. He is said to be in heaven not definitively, as if he were not elsewhere at the same time, but manifestatively; and this not simply, but only as regards eminence, because there chiefly shine forth the rays of his majesty and glory. Isa. 66. 1. Psal. 19. 1. &c.

units.la: A. Si Deus Sanctus sit & bonus, cur peccatum & mala tot inde consequentia in mundo passim grassari finit?
units.tr: A. If God is holy and good, why does he allow sin and the many evils that follow from it to spread everywhere in the world?

units.la: B. Peccati mala consequentia non permittit modo, sed infligit, impiis ex justitia, piis ex disciplina & charitate paterna. Peccatum permittit (hoc est non impedit) ut sapiens mundi gubernator, non permittit impure, ut justissimus mundi judex.
units.tr: B. He does not merely permit the evil consequences of sin; he inflicts them, on the impious out of justice, and on the pious through fatherly discipline and love. He permits sin (that is, does not prevent it) as the wise governor of the world, but he does not permit it unjustly as the most just judge of the world.

units.la: A. Qui potest summa justitia cum summa misericordia conciliari?
units.tr: A. How can supreme justice be reconciled with supreme mercy?

units.la: B. Si quæritur de habitibus (ita enim humano more loquendum est cum in Deo proprie sunt nulli) utraque cum altera optime consentit, & quasi coincidit in una Dei simplicissima essentia, eaque perfectissima.
units.tr: B. If the question concerns habits (for we must speak in human fashion, since in God there are properly none), the two agree very well with each other and, as it were, coincide in the one most simple and most perfect essence of God.

units.la: A. Quæro potius de actibus.
units.tr: A. I ask rather about acts.

units.la: B. Neque sic vel minimum repugnant, si ad objecta diversa referantur, v. g. actus summæ justitiæ
units.tr: B. Neither do they conflict in the slightest, if they are referred to different objects. For example, the act of supreme justice

units.la: justitiae stitiæ (vindicantem hic intelligimus) erga Christum mediatorem, conjunctus est cum actu summæ misericordiæ erga hominem peccatorem. Is. 53.4,5.
units.tr: (here we understand the avenging act) toward Christ the mediator is joined with the act of supreme mercy toward the sinful human being. Is. 53.4,5.

units.la: A. Num Deus certissimè cognoscit futura contingentia?
units.tr: A. Does God know future contingent things with the greatest certainty?

units.la: B. Omnino; quod innumera docent in Scripturis exempla: qualia sunt ista, Exod. 3. 19. Deut. 31.20, 21, 22.
units.tr: B. Altogether; innumerable examples in Scripture teach this, such as these: Exod. 3. 19. Deut. 31.20, 21, 22.

units.la: A. Quodnam est obiectum potentiæ Divinæ?
units.tr: A. What is the object of divine power?

units.la: B. Quicquid a vult facere; & quod neque contradictionem implicat, nec infinitæ ejus b persectioni adversatur. a Ps. 135. 6. b Tit. 1. 2. Heb. 6. 18.
units.tr: B. Whatever he wills to do, provided that it neither implies a contradiction nor opposes his infinite perfection. a Ps. 135. 6. b Tit. 1. 2. Heb. 6. 18.

units.la: A. Ea vero proprietatum in Deo congeries, nonne compositionem indicat, & consequenter ejus simplicitati derogat?
units.tr: A. Does that collection of properties in God not indicate composition, and consequently detract from his simplicity?

units.la: B. Nequaquam. Sunt enim istæ proprietates neque ab essentia Divina, neque à se invicem realiter disjunctæ: unde nec ullam inferunt compositionem, nisi unius rationis, quæ naturæ simplici minime repugnat.
units.tr: B. By no means. For these properties are neither really distinct from the divine essence nor really distinct from one another. Hence they introduce no composition except one of reason alone, which is in no way repugnant to a simple nature.

units.la: Cap. 3. De tribus in essentia Divina Personis.
units.tr: Chap. 3. Concerning the three Persons in the Divine essence.

units.la: A. ESne unus tantum Deus?
units.tr: A. Is there only one God?

units.la: B. Plane; quod & Scriptura passim clamat, & ratio naturalis evincit, quippe cui plura infinita repugnant.
units.tr: B. Plainly so; Scripture proclaims this everywhere, and natural reason proves it, since several infinite beings are incompatible with it.

units.la: A. Verum afferente Apostolo Dii sunt multi?
units.tr: A. But does the Apostle say that there are many gods?

units.la: B. Sed nobis, ibidem inquit, est unus tantum Deus; proinde intelligendus est de diis Ethnicorum putatitiis, vel de Vicariis illis & metaphoricis, quales sunt Magistratus & Principes terreni.
units.tr: B. But he says there, "For us there is only one God." Therefore it must be understood of the supposed gods of the heathen, or of those vicarious and metaphorical gods, such as magistrates and earthly princes.

units.la: A. At in ista summa unitate nonne continetur Trinitas Personarum?
units.tr: A. But does not the Trinity of Persons lie within this supreme unity?

units.la: B. Id quidem firmiter credendum est, cum Scrip. toties diserte inculcet, & Ecclesia Christiana ab ipsis jam inde Evangelii incunabilis ad haec usque tempora agnoverit.
units.tr: B. This indeed must be firmly believed, since Scripture so often inculcates it in plain terms, and the Christian Church has acknowledged it from the very cradle of the Gospel down to the present times.

units.la: A. Quibus internoscuntur nominibus tres illae personae?
units.tr: A. By what names are those three Persons distinguished?

units.la: B. Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: B. As the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: A. Ast ubi vel Trinitatis vel personarum in Scripturis mentio?
units.tr: A. But where is there mention of the Trinity or of the Persons in Scripture?

units.la: B. Trinitatis (secundum versionem Anglicanam) expressa habetur 1 Jo. 5. 7. Quod si quis de ista versione litem moverit, non est magnopere laborandum.
units.tr: B. The Trinity is expressly stated in 1 John 5. 7, according to the English version. If anyone raises a dispute about that version, it is not necessary to labour the point greatly.

units.la: A. Quidni? stitiæ (vindicantem hic intelligimus) erga Christum mediatorem, conjunctus est cum actu summæ misericordiæ erga hominem peccatorem. Is. 53.4,5.
units.tr: A. Why not? Justice (here understood as avenging) towards Christ the Mediator is joined with an act of supreme mercy towards sinful man. Is. 53. 4, 5.

units.la: A. Num Deus certissimè cognoscit futura contingentia?
units.tr: A. Does God know future contingent things with the most certain knowledge?

units.la: B. Omnino; quod innumera docent in Scripturis exempla: qualia sunt ista, Exod. 3. 19. Deut. 31.20, 21, 22.
units.tr: B. Certainly; countless examples in Scripture teach this, such as these: Exod. 3. 19; Deut. 31. 20, 21, 22.

units.la: A. Quodnam est objectum potentiæ Divinæ?
units.tr: A. What is the object of the divine power?

units.la: B. Quicquid a vult facere; & quod neque contradictionem implicat, nec infinitæ ejus b persectioni adversatur. a Ps. 135. 6. b Tit. 1. 2. Heb. 6. 18.
units.tr: B. Whatever he wills to do, and which neither implies a contradiction nor runs counter to his infinite perfection. a Ps. 135. 6. b Tit. 1. 2. Heb. 6. 18.

units.la: A. Ea vero proprietatum in Deo congeries, nonne compositionem indicat, & consequenter ejus simplicitati derogat?
units.tr: A. Does not this collection of properties in God indicate composition, and consequently detract from his simplicity?

units.la: B. Nequaquam. Sunt enim istæ proprietates neque ab essentia Divina, neque à se invicem realiter disjunctæ: unde nec ullam inferunt compositionem, nisi unius rationis, quæ naturæ simplici minime repugnat.
units.tr: B. By no means. For these properties are neither really separate from the divine essence nor from one another; hence they introduce no composition, except of a single kind of reason, which in no way conflicts with a simple nature.

units.la: Cap. 3. De tribus in essentia Divina Personis.
units.tr: Chapter 3. On the Three Persons in the Divine Essence.

units.la: A. EStne unus tantum Deus ?
units.tr: A. Is there only one God?

units.la: B. Plane ; quod & Scriptura passim clamat, & ratio naturalis evincit, quippe cui plura infinita repugnant.
units.tr: B. Plainly so; Scripture cries this out everywhere, and natural reason proves it, since countless infinite absurdities would contradict any other view.

units.la: A. Verum asserente Apostolo Dii sunt multi ?
units.tr: A. But the Apostle asserts that there are many gods?

units.la: B. Sed nobis, ibidem inquit, est unus tantum Deus ; proinde intelligendus est de diis Ethnicorum putatitiis, vel de Vicariis illis & metaphoricis,a quales sunt Magistratus & Principes terreni. a Exod. 22. 28.
units.tr: B. But in the same place he says, "for us there is only one God." Therefore it must be understood of the so-called gods of the heathen, or of those vicegerents and metaphorical gods, such as magistrates and earthly princes. Exod. 22. 28.

units.la: A. At in ista summa unitate nonne continetur Trinitas Personarum ?
units.tr: A. But does not this supreme unity contain the Trinity of Persons?

units.la: B. Id quidem firmiter credendum est, cum Scrip. toties diserte inculcet, & Ecclesia Christiana ab ipsis jam inde Evangelii incunabilis ad hæc usque tempora agnoverit.
units.tr: B. That indeed is to be firmly believed, since Scripture so often insists on it in plain words, and the Christian Church has acknowledged it from the very cradle of the Gospel down to these times.

units.la: A. Quibus internoscuntur nominibus tres illæ personæ ?
units.tr: A. By what names are those three persons distinguished?

units.la: B. Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus Sancti.
units.tr: B. Of the Father, of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: A. Ast ubi vel Trinitatis vel personarum in Scripturis mentio ?
units.tr: A. But where in the Scriptures is there mention of the Trinity or of the persons?

units.la: B. Trinitatis (secundum versionem Anglicanam) expressa habetur 1 Jo. 5. 7. Quod si quis de ista versione litem moverit, non est magnopere laborandum.
units.tr: B. The Trinity is expressly found in 1 Jo. 5. 7, according to the English version. If anyone raises a dispute about that version, it is not worth labouring over too much.

units.la: A. Quidni?
units.tr: A. Why not?

units.la: B. Utpote cum gloriosissimæ illius Triadis personæ singulæ conjunctim, & æquali honore præditæ legantur; singularum Deitati seorsim à reliquis testimonia sat multa perhibeant aliæ Scripturæ. Mat. 28. 19.
units.tr: B. Since the persons of that most glorious Triad are read of together and endowed with equal honour; and other Scriptures give quite enough testimony to the Deity of each of them separately from the others. Mat. 28. 19.

units.la: A. De Persona vocabulo quid censes?
units.tr: A. What do you think of the word "person"?

units.la: B. Id quoque reperitur, Heb. 1. 3. Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ aliorumque doctissimorum Interpretum suffragio communitum: ejusque in hoc negotio usus ab Ecclesia Catholica comprobatur.
units.tr: B. That too is found, Heb. 1. 3, and is supported by the agreement of the English Church and of other most learned interpreters; and its use in this matter is approved by the Catholic Church.

units.la: A. Quid vero si quis hic etiam contentiosus esse velit?
units.tr: A. But what if someone here also wishes to be contentious?

units.la: B. De re ipsa convinci poterit (nisi contradicendi studio, ut fit, abreptus) ex locutionibus illis Scripturalibus, quæ nisi personis accommodari nequeunt.
units.tr: B. He can be convinced of the matter itself (unless he is carried away by a zeal for contradiction, as often happens) from those Scriptural expressions which can be applied only to persons.

units.la: A. Cedo illarum aliquot.
units.tr: A. Name some of them.

units.la: B. Sufficerit unica de Spiritu Sancto, cum & eadem erit reliquarum ratio, ejusque personalitatem potissimum oppugnant Trinitatis adversarii. Is, etsi nomen ei Græcum sit alterius generis, cum masculino tamen pronomine conjunctus legitur, quod, nisi persona esset, folæco laboraret. ἐκεῖνος, τὸ πνεῦμα. Joh. 16. 3. adde quod dicitur docere, dona dare, velle, &c. quæ unius personæ sunt. 1 Joh. 16. 1 Cor. 12.
units.tr: B. One concerning the Holy Spirit will suffice, since the reasoning for the rest will be the same; and the adversaries of the Trinity chiefly attack his personality. Although his name is Greek and of another gender, he is nevertheless read joined with a masculine pronoun, which would be pointless unless he were a person: he [ἐκεῖνος], the Spirit [τὸ πνεῦμα]. Joh. 16. 3. Add that he is said to teach, to give gifts, to will, and so on, which belong to one person only. 1 Joh. 16. 1 Cor. 12.

units.la: A. Unde constat Christum non esse nudum hominem?
units.tr: A. How do we know that Christ is not a mere man?

units.la: B. Quoniam si talis esset, sequeretur eum tunc primum extitisse, cum ex Virgine Maria nasceretur: at ex Scripturarum perplurium clariffima luce evincitur contrarium, Jo. 1. 2, 3. Jo. 8. 58. Gal. 4. 4. Phil. 2. 7, &c.
units.tr: B. Because if he were such, it would follow that he first existed when he was born of the Virgin Mary; but the clearest light of very many Scriptures proves the contrary. Jo. 1. 2, 3. Jo. 8. 58. Gal. 4. 4. Phil. 2. 7, etc.

units.la: A. Quî vero constabit eum esse verum, & aeternum Deum?
units.tr: A. But how will it be established that he is the true and eternal God?

units.la: B. Ex nomine, proprietatibus, & operibus Divinis.
units.tr: B. From his name, his properties, and his divine works.

units.la: A. Incipias à nomine.
units.tr: A. Begin with the name.

units.la: B. 1. Nomen ei incommunicabile Jehovae tribuitur, ut Joh. 12. 41. collat. cum Isaiae 6. 3.
units.tr: B. 1. The incommunicable name Jehovah is ascribed to him, as in Joh. 12. 41, compared with Isaiah 6. 3.

units.la: 1 Cor. 10. 9. collat. cum Num. 21. 6. 2° dicitur Deus benedictus in saecula, Ro. 9. 5. Dominus & Deus à Sancto Thoma agnitus, Jo. 20. 28. verus Deus à Sancto Johanne, 1 Joh. 5. 20. Æqualis Deo, Phil. 2. 6. Magnus ille Deus, Tit. 2. 13.
units.tr: 1 Cor. 10. 9, compared with Num. 21. 6. Second, he is called God blessed for ever, Rom. 9. 5; Lord and God, as acknowledged by St Thomas, Jo. 20. 28; true God, according to St John, 1 Joh. 5. 20; equal to God, Phil. 2. 6; that great God, Tit. 2. 13.

units.la: A. Perge ad ejus proprietates Divinas.
units.tr: A. Go on to his divine properties.

units.la: B. 1. Est Æternus, primus, & ultimus, Apoc. 1. 17. collat. cum Is. 44. 6. Joh. 8. 58.
units.tr: B. 1. He is eternal, the first and the last, Apoc. 1. 17, compared with Isaiah 44. 6; Joh. 8. 58.

units.la: 2. Est omnniscius, Joh. 21. 17. Apoc. 2. 23. collat. cum Jer. 17. 9, 10.
units.tr: 2. He is omniscient, Joh. 21. 17; Apoc. 2. 23, compared with Jer. 17. 9, 10.

units.la: 3. Est omnipotens, quod testantur miracula varia sua solius virtute edita, ut Mat. 8. 3. 16. & alibi in Evangelio passim.
units.tr: 3. He is omnipotent, as his various miracles, performed by his own power alone, attest: Mat. 8. 3. 16., and elsewhere throughout the Gospel.

units.la: 4. Est adorandus, Heb. 1. 6. collat. cum Apoc. 19. 10.
units.tr: 4. He is to be adored, Heb. 1. 6, compared with Apoc. 19. 10.

units.la: A. Superest ut opera quoque ejus Divina in medium proferantur.
units.tr: A. It remains that his divine works also be brought forward.

units.la: B. 1. Est Creator omnium, Heb. 3. 3, 4. Jo. 1. 3.
units.tr: B. 1. He is the Creator of all things, Heb. 3. 3, 4; Joh. 1. 3.

units.la: 2. Est conservator omnium, Heb. 1. 3. collat. cum Ps. 36. 6.
units.tr: 2. He is the preserver of all things, Heb. 1. 3, compared with Ps. 36. 6.

units.la: 3. Divina edidit miracula dum in terris ageret, ut supra, vid. Joh. 15. 24. inter quæ præcipuum erat refuscitatio sui ipsius à mortuis, Joh. 2. 19, 21. & c. 10. 18.
units.tr: 3. While he was on earth he performed divine miracles, as above; see Joh. 15. 24. Among these the chief was his own resurrection from the dead, Joh. 2. 19, 21; and c. 10. 18.

units.la: 4. Confert vitam æternam, Joh. 10. 28, collat. cum 30.
units.tr: 4. He bestows eternal life, Joh. 10. 28, compared with 30.

units.la: A. Unde liquet Spiritum Sanctum esse verum Deum?
units.tr: A. Whence is it clear that the Holy Spirit is the true God?

units.la: B. 1. Ita diserte appellatur, 1 Cor. 3. 16. Acts 5. 3, 4.
units.tr: B. 1. He is so expressly called, 1 Cor. 3. 16; Act. 5. 3, 4.

units.la: 2. Insignitur proprietatibus Divinis, a æternitate, b omnipræsentia, c omniscientia. a Heb. 9. 14. b Ps. 139. 7. c 1 Cor. 2. 10.
units.tr: 2. He is marked with divine properties: (a) eternity, (b) omnipresence, (c) omniscience. (a) Heb. 9. 14. (b) Ps. 139. 7. (c) 1 Cor. 2. 10.

units.la: 3. Facit Opera divina, qualia sunt a collatio donorum cœlestium pro suo ipsius beneplacito, b effectio miraculorum, & alia hujusmodi. a 1 Cor. 12. 4. 11. b Mat. 12. 28.
units.tr: 3. He performs divine works, such as (a) the bestowal of heavenly gifts according to his own good pleasure, (b) the working of miracles, and others of this kind. (a) 1 Cor. 12. 4, 11. (b) Mat. 12. 28.

units.la: A. Quod si Spiritus Sanctus sit Deus, quomodo dicuntur fideles impleri Spiritu, ut Stephanus, Act. 6?
units.tr: A. But if the Holy Spirit is God, how are the faithful said to be filled with the Spirit, as Stephen was, Act. 6?

units.la: B. Istæ locutiones sunt Metonymicæ, quibus non persona, sed dona Spiritus gratuita notantur.
units.tr: B. Those expressions are metonymical, by which not the person but the gifts of the Spirit are denoted.

units.la: Cap. 4. De Providentia Divina.
units.tr: Chapter 4. On Divine Providence.

units.la: A. Quid est providentia Dei?
units.tr: A. What is the providence of God?

units.la: B. Est qua res omnes creatas potentia sua sustentat, sapientia moderatur ac regit. Heb. 1. 3. Act. 17. 28. Eph. 1. 11.
units.tr: B. It is that by which God sustains all created things by his power and governs and directs them by his wisdom. Heb. 1. 3. Acts 17. 28. Eph. 1. 11.

units.la: A. An vero res etiam minima intra hujus providentiae ambitum versantur?
units.tr: A. But do even the smallest things fall within the scope of this providence?

units.la: B. Sic est, attestante tum Scriptura, tum ratione. Mat. 10. 29, 30. consulantur miracula Ægyptiaca in lib. Exod. vid. Job 38. & Psal. 147 &c.
units.tr: B. They do, as both Scripture and reason attest. Matt. 10. 29, 30. Consult the Egyptian plagues in the book of Exodus; see Job 38 and Ps. 147, etc.

units.la: A. Sed quanam hoc suadet ratio?
units.tr: A. But what reason suggests this?

units.la: B. Si de minimis istis à Deo conservandis quaeritur, ratio haud obscura est à majori, quoniam scil. ab influxu divino creaturae praestantissimae dependent, (quod extra controversiam est) nedum vilissimae. Mat. 6. 26. 30.
units.tr: B. If the question is about these smallest things that God preserves, the reasoning is not obscure, drawn from the greater: namely, that the most excellent creatures depend on the divine influence (which is beyond dispute), let alone the most worthless. Matt. 6. 26, 30.

units.la: A. Cur vero res tantula statuantur objectum moderaminis seu gubernationis divinae?
units.tr: A. But why are such trifling things made the object of the divine government or guidance?

units.la: B. Scilicet alias frustra condiderat.
units.tr: B. Because otherwise God would have created them in vain.

units.la: A. In quibus autem creaturis praecipue elucet providentia Dei?
units.tr: A. In which creatures does the providence of God especially shine forth?

units.la: B. In Angelis & Hominibus, bonis & malis.
units.tr: B. In angels and men, both good and evil.

units.la: A. In bonis quomodo Hominibus?
units.tr: A. How in good men?

units.la: B. Quod illos in benevolentiae paternae sinu complectitur, & per varias tandem vitae praesentis aerumnas & discrimina ad aeternae felicitatis portum tutos perducit, Jer. 31. 20. Mat. 7. 11. Act. 4. 22.
units.tr: B. Because he embraces them in the bosom of his fatherly goodwill, and at last, through the various hardships and dangers of the present life, brings them safe to the harbour of eternal blessedness. Jer. 31. 20. Matt. 7. 11. Acts 4. 22.

units.la: A. Qui in malis?
units.tr: A. And in the wicked?

units.la: B. Quod illorum malitiam (sibi intime antefacula perspectam) 1. Etsi possit, minime, tamen impediat. 2. (Ex fe interminabilem) certis pro suo solius arbitrio limitibus coerceat. 3. Quod in piorum bonum, & nominis fui gloriam mirifice (quasi reluctantem) trahit. Et 4. Horrendis demum Gehennae cruciatibus (iisque aeternis) in peccatorem animadvertit.
units.tr: B. In that (1) although he could, he by no means prevents their malice, which he sees thoroughly in his own mind as a torch; (2) he restrains it, which in itself is boundless, within limits fixed by his own will alone; (3) he wonderfully draws it, as though reluctant, to the good of the godly and to the glory of his name; and (4) finally he punishes the sinner with the dreadful torments of Gehenna, and those eternal.

units.la: A. Quod si Deus permittit impiorum grassari malitiam, cur dicitur Deus nolens iniquitatem? Psal. 5. 5.
units.tr: A. But if God permits the malice of the impious to run riot, why is God said to be one who is not willing iniquity? Ps. 5. 5.

units.la: B. Si teneretur impedire, utrumque de eo dici non potest: vult itaque voluntate tantum permittente, quoad actus alicujus aut habitus malitiam, non vult voluntate ant imperante aut efficiente; imo odit, prohibet, punit. & (ex parte) semper coercet. Acts 13. 18.
units.tr: B. If he were bound to prevent it, neither statement could be made of him. He therefore wills the malice of some act or habit only by permitting; he does not will it by commanding or effecting. Indeed he hates it, forbids it, punishes it, and (in part) always restrains it. Acts 13. 18.

units.la: A. At cum dicitur indurare corda, annon hinc sequetur Deum esse Authorem peccati?
units.tr: A. But when it is said that he hardens hearts, does it not follow from this that God is the author of sin?

units.la: B. Absit; Nam ex mollibus dura non efficit, sed gratiam indebitam & nihili habitam subtrahendo, durefcere, idque magis magisque justissimus finit Judex. Exod. 3. 19. 7. 23. 8. 15, 32. Rom. 11. 35. Psal. 81. 11, 12. Isa. 5. 6. Hos. 4. 17.
units.tr: B. Far from it. For he does not make soft hearts hard; rather, by withdrawing the undeserved grace that was held as nothing, the most just Judge allows them to harden more and more. Exod. 3. 19; 7. 23; 8. 15, 32. Rom. 11. 35. Ps. 81. 11, 12. Isa. 5. 6. Hos. 4. 17.

units.la: A. An demum cum providentia divina libertas stabit humana?
units.tr: A. Finally, does human freedom stand together with divine providence?

units.la: B. Admodum; quod communis tam bonorum, quam malorum indicat experientia; utrique que enim hi malè, illi b bene, ex animi proposito & libera voluntatis electione agunt. a Pro. 1: 30, 31. Is. 66. 3. b Ps. 119. 30.
units.tr: B. Entirely so; common experience of good and bad alike shows this, for the one group acts wickedly and the other well, from a purpose of the mind and by free choice of the will. Prov. 1. 30, 31. Isa. 66. 3. Ps. 119. 30.

units.la: A. Nullam ergo inducit necessitatem providentia?
units.tr: A. Does providence therefore bring in no necessity?

units.la: B. Quæ libertatem adimat, nullam: i. e. 1° neque coactionis, neque 2° absolutam, (qualis est agentium purè naturalium) sed necessitatem infallibilitatis & merè hypotheticam, (a respectu nimirum habito ad Deum infallibilem) inferre palam est; neque hæc b ullatenus cum libertate creaturæ pugnat. a Num. 23. 8, 19. Mat. 24. 6. b Act. 4. 28. collat. cum Act. 3. 14.
units.tr: B. None that would take away freedom. That is, it plainly brings in neither (1) a necessity of compulsion, nor (2) an absolute necessity (such as that of purely natural agents), but only a necessity of infallibility and merely hypothetical (namely, arising from the relation to an infallible God). And this in no way conflicts with the freedom of the creature. Num. 23. 8, 19. Matt. 24. 6. Acts 4. 28, compared with Acts 3. 14.

units.la: Cap. 5. De creatione primi Hominis, & de fœdere primo cum eodem sancito.
units.tr: Chapter 5. On the creation of the first man, and on the first covenant sanctioned with him.

units.la: A. UNde constat Adamum fuisse primum hominem?
units.tr: A. How is it established that Adam was the first man?

units.la: B. Ex historia luculenta Creationis, Gen. 1. collata cum Gen. 2. 19, &c. necnon ex Luc. 3. 38. ubi idcirco dicitur filius Dei, utpote alium (sicut reliqui) non habens patrem.
units.tr: B. From the clear account of the Creation in Gen. 1, compared with Gen. 2:19 etc., and also from Luke 3:38, where for this reason he is called the son of God, since, unlike the rest of us, he had no father.

units.la: A. Cur dicitur conditus ad imaginem Dei?
units.tr: A. Why is he said to have been made in the image of God?

units.la: B. 1. Non ratione partis corporeæ, cum Deus sit Spiritus: at 2°, quoad dotes & virtutes animæ, quà morales, quà intellectuales, imo & totius animæ sanctitatem, quam ei largitus est Deus. Eph. 4. 24.
units.tr: B. (1) Not with respect to a bodily part, since God is Spirit; but (2) with respect to the gifts and virtues of the soul, both moral and intellectual, and indeed the holiness of the whole soul, which God bestowed on him. Eph. 4:24.

units.la: A. Verum sic & conditi sunt Angeli?
units.tr: A. But were the angels also created in this way?

units.la: B. Sanè; proinde quod in ista imagine divina peculiare erat homini, est dominium in reliquas creaturas sublunares vicarium, Gen. 1.26.collat. cum Gen. 2. 20.
units.tr: B. Certainly. Yet what was peculiar to man within this divine image was dominion over the other creatures of the lower world, exercised as God's deputy. Gen. 1:26, compared with Gen. 2:20.

units.la: A. Num tenebatur Deus Adamum in isto statu primævo perseverantem mercede aut præmio donare?
units.tr: A. Was God obliged to reward Adam with wages or a prize, had he persevered in that primal state?

units.la: B. Nullatenus; quia Dei ad creaturam nulla potest esse obligatio, nisi voluntaria.
units.tr: B. By no means; for God can owe nothing to a creature except voluntarily.

units.la: A. An ergo tali posita perseverantia ullam habuit Adamus spem præmii?
units.tr: A. Then, given such perseverance, did Adam have any hope of a reward?

units.la: B. Omnino; sed ex solo fœdere, quod lubens cum eo pepigit Deus.
units.tr: B. Entirely so; but only from the covenant, which God gladly made with him.

units.la: A. Unde vero constiterit ullum tale fœdus Deo intercessisse cum Adamo? B. Ni-
units.tr: A. But how do we know that any such covenant was made between God and Adam? B. Ni-

units.la: B. Nimirum dictat ratio adfuisse omnia ad fœdus requisita.
units.tr: B. Namely, reason dictates that all the things required for a covenant were present.

units.la: A. Dic, ista.
units.tr: A. Tell me these things.

units.la: B. Mutuum intelligo consensum, & stipulationem utriusque partis.
units.tr: B. I understand a mutual consent and an agreement (stipulation) of both parties.

units.la: A. De Deo fatis liquet; sed de Adamo, quâ efficis ratione?
units.tr: A. It is fairly clear regarding God; but regarding Adam, by what reasoning do you prove it?

units.la: B. Consensus quidem disertis verbis habetur nullus, at talem aliquem fuisse optima ratione nititur.
units.tr: B. Indeed, no consent is found in express words; yet it is argued on the best grounds that some such consent existed.

units.la: A. Credo istam.
units.tr: A. I believe that.

units.la: B. Si enim ex parte Adami deficeret hæc ftipulatio, sequeretur aut conditionem ab eo præstandam (viz. obedientiam) aut præmium à Deo promissum ei minus placuisse, quorum utrumque cum supposita ejus integritate (tum intellectus tum voluntatis) omnino pugnat.
units.tr: B. For if this agreement were lacking on Adam's side, it would follow either that the condition he was to fulfil (namely obedience) or the reward promised him by God would have been less pleasing to him; and both of these are wholly inconsistent with his supposed integrity, both of intellect and of will.

units.la: A. Quid ab homine præstandum exigebat illud fœdus?
units.tr: A. What did that covenant require to be performed by man?

units.la: B. Perfectam utique numeris omnibus & perfonalem voluntati Divinæ præstandam obedientiam, Gal. 3. 10. unde & fœdus operum usitato dicitur.
units.tr: B. Perfect obedience, in every respect, and personal, rendered to the divine will. Gal. 3:10. Hence it is also commonly called the covenant of works.

units.la: A. Quæ merces promissa obsequenti?
units.tr: A. What reward was promised to the one who obeyed?

units.la: B. Fælix & læta immortalitas, ceu vita æterna. Gal. 3. 12.
units.tr: B. A happy and joyful immortality, such as eternal life. Gal. 3:12.

units.la: A. Quæ pœna peccanti denunciata?
units.tr: A. What punishment was threatened for the one who sinned?

units.la: B. Mors, Gen. 2. qua a omne genus miseria (etiam b æterna continetur) quæque consequenter c ante peccatum nullo sensu erat naturalis aut necessaria. a Psal. 44.22. 1Cor.15.31. b Ezek.18 20,21,23, &c. Ro. 6.23. c Ro. 5.12.
units.tr: B. Death, Gen. 2, which includes every kind of misery (even eternal misery), and which accordingly, before sin, was in no sense natural or necessary. Ps. 44:22; 1 Cor. 15:31; Ezek. 18:20, 21, 23, etc.; Rom. 6:23; Rom. 5:12.

units.la: Cap. 6. De peccato, sive Lapsu Hominis, & miseriis consequentibus.
units.tr: Chapter 6. Of sin, or the fall of man, and the miseries that follow.

units.la: A. Qui potuit Homo, cum esset conditus ad imaginem Dei, descisçere à Deo?
units.tr: A. How could man, who was created in the image of God, fall away from God?

units.la: B. Ex pravo liberi Arbitrii usu, quod & lapsus Angelorum causa.
units.tr: B. Through the wrong use of free choice, which was also the cause of the fall of the angels.

units.la: A. An ergo nullam ei necessitatem peccandi imposuit Deus?
units.tr: A. Did God then impose no necessity of sinning on him?

units.la: B. Omnino nullam, qui & gratiam illi qua peccatum repelleret sufficientem impertivit, nec datam nisi à peccante revocavit, Eccles. 7. 29.
units.tr: B. None at all. He gave him sufficient grace by which he could resist sin, and he withdrew the grace he had given only from the one who sinned. Eccles. 7. 29.

units.la: A. At potuit Adamum Deus, quo minus peccaret, uberiore gratia donare?
units.tr: A. But could God have given Adam a fuller grace, so that he would not have sinned?

units.la: B. Nihil verius; sed neque ad hoc ullatenus tenebatur, neque sic infinitæ suæ sapientiæ visum est, quod eventus docet. Mat. 20. 15.
units.tr: B. Nothing is more true; but God was not bound to do this in any way, and it did not seem good to his infinite wisdom to do so, as the outcome shows. Matt. 20. 15.

units.la: A. Dic mala ipsius peccati primi consequentia.
units.tr: A. Tell me the evil consequences of this first sin itself.

units.la: B. Ea in duplici discrimine reperiuntur: sunt enim alia temporanea (in hoc præsente sæculo) æterna alia, in futuro.
units.tr: B. They are of two kinds: some are temporal, in this present age, and others are eternal, in the age to come.

units.la: A. Da primi generis.
units.tr: A. Give me the first kind.

units.la: B. Illa rursus aut corporis sunt, aut animi.
units.tr: B. These in turn are either of the body or of the soul.

units.la: A. Quanam ea sunt corporis mala?
units.tr: A. What are the evils of the body?

units.la: B. Caduca ejusdem temperies, morbi, ærumnæ variæ, mors demum ipsa.
units.tr: B. A frail constitution of the body, disease, various hardships, and finally death itself.

units.la: A. An itaque à morbis & morte immunis extitisset homo, si non peccasset?
units.tr: A. So would man have been free from disease and death if he had not sinned?

units.la: B. Prorsus.
units.tr: B. Entirely.

units.la: B. a Prorsus; ex gratia tamen divina, magis quam ex conditione corporis,etsi præstantissima. a Ro. 5. 12.
units.tr: B. Entirely; yet this was by divine grace, rather than by the condition of the body, although that was most excellent. Rom. 5. 12.

units.la: A. Quanam sunt animi mala peccatum secuta?
units.tr: A. What evils of the soul followed sin?

units.la: B. Ea multo triftiora, per omnes illius facultates disseminata : a error scilicet in judicio, b pravitas in appetitu & c affectibus, lubricitas (ad bonum) d memoriæ, e vitiosa conscientiæ temperies, ejufdemque ex admisso peccato f cruciatus, g totius denique Hominis ad peccatum pronitas, hisque omnibus adjuncta h subjectio Diabolo, & ira Dei. a 1 Cor. 2. 14. Eph. 5. 8. b Joh. 1. 13. Ro. 7. 19. c Jer. 11. 15. Ro. 1. 25. ad finem. d Deut. 32. 18. e Eph. 4. 19. Jer. 2. 35. f Gen. 3. 8, 10, &c. 42. 21. Mat. 27. 4, 5. g Job. 15 16. Eph. 4. 19. h Eph. 2. 2, 3.
units.tr: B. They are much more grievous, spread through all his faculties: (1) error, namely in judgment; (2) perversity in appetite and in the affections; (3) slipperiness toward the good in the memory; (4) a corrupt disposition of the conscience, and the torment of that conscience because of sin committed; (5) finally, the proneness of the whole man to sin; and joined with all these, (6) subjection to the Devil, and (7) the wrath of God. 1 Cor. 2. 14. Eph. 5. 8. John 1. 13. Rom. 7. 19. Jer. 11. 15. Rom. 1. 25 to the end. Deut. 32. 18. Eph. 4. 19. Jer. 2. 35. Gen. 3. 8, 10, &c. 42. 21. Matt. 27. 4, 5. Job 15. 16. Eph. 4. 19. Eph. 2. 2, 3.

units.la: A. Num hinc sequetur amissse Hominem pec- catorem Liberi Arbitrii usum?
units.tr: A. Does it follow from this that sinful man has lost the use of free choice?

units.la: B. Non circa res civiles, aut vitæ cotidianæ negotia, testante experientia; quanquam in his quoque multum abest ab ista perspicacitate mentis & affectuum rectitudine, quæ ad plenum libertatis usum requiruntur.
units.tr: B. Not in civil affairs or the ordinary business of life, as experience testifies; although even in these he is far from that clarity of mind and rectitude of affections which are required for the full use of liberty.

units.la: A. In rebus pure spiritualibus quid potest?
units.tr: A. What can he do in purely spiritual matters?

units.la: B. Non est negandum Hominem liberè facere, quod fecundum voluntatem facit, five bonum, a five malum: sed antequam regenitus fit in hominem spiritualem, neque b sapit, neque facit, quod gratum est Deo. a Pro. 1. 29, 30. Is. 66. 4. b 1 Cor. 12. 14. Ro. 8. 7. c Heb. 11. 6.
units.tr: B. It must not be denied that man does freely whatever he does according to his will, whether good or evil; but before he is born again into a spiritual man, he neither understands nor does what is pleasing to God. Prov. 1. 29, 30. Isa. 66. 4. 1 Cor. 12. 14. Rom. 8. 7. Heb. 11. 6.

units.la: A. Dic mala ista, quæ vocas æterna, in seculo futuro?
units.tr: A. Tell me those evils which you call eternal, in the age to come.

units.la: B. Ea quidem pro magnitudine facis exprimi non possunt: sed in genere ad binas pœnæ classes revocantur, damni scilicet & sensus.
units.tr: B. By their greatness they cannot indeed be expressed, but in general they are reduced to two classes of punishment, namely of loss and of sense.

units.la: A. Utriusque naturam explica.
units.tr: A. Explain the nature of each.

units.la: B. Pœna damni est æterna peccatoris à fede & gaudiis Beatorum exclusio. Pœna sensus est horribilis ille tum corporis tum animæ in Gehenna cruciatus cum Diabolo & Angelis ejus, Mat. 25.41. 2 Thess. 1, 8, 9.
units.tr: B. The punishment of loss is the eternal exclusion of the sinner from the vision and joys of the blessed. The punishment of sense is that dreadful torment of both body and soul in Gehenna, along with the Devil and his angels. Matt. 25. 41. 2 Thess. 1. 8, 9.

units.la: A. Cur vero tam levi (in specie) peccato tam gravis incubuit pœna?
units.tr: A. But why has so heavy a punishment fallen on a sin so slight in its kind?

units.la: B. Ob laesam eo majestatem infinitam. Quin etsi ad aspectum non satis intuenti (quoad materiam) levius videatur, erat tamen reapse (perpensis circumstantiis) flagitiosissimum, imo peccatorum potius infanda congeries, quam simplex peccatum.
units.tr: B. Because by it the infinite majesty was injured. Indeed, although to a glance that does not look closely it may seem lighter as regards its matter, it was in fact (when the circumstances are weighed) most scandalous; nay, it was rather an unspeakable heap of sins than a single sin.

units.la: A. Hæccine ad primos tantum parentes manavit peccati lues, an vero ad omnes illorum posteros derivata grassatur?
units.tr: A. Did this plague of sin spread only to the first parents, or has it been passed on and does it rage among all their descendants?

units.la: B. Imo, cum ob communem culpæ a societatem virtualem, tum ob contagium b personale nemo hominum eadem calamitate implicitus non tenetur, Christo ἀνθρώπῳ duntaxat excepto, quique per Christum æterna morte liberantur. aRo. 5. 12. 15. &c. bJob. 14. 4. Joh. 3, 6.
units.tr: B. Indeed, no man is free from this same calamity, both because of the common participation in guilt, which is virtual, and because of personal contagion; only Christ as man is excepted, and those who are freed through Christ from eternal death. Rom. 5. 12, 15, &c. Job 14. 4. John 3. 6.

units.la: A. Unde Posteris oritur ista culpa societas cum Parente πρωτοπλάστῳ?
units.tr: A. From what does this sharing of guilt with the first-formed parent arise for the posterity?

units.la: B. Ex Adami conditione singulorum repræsentativa, quippe qui non privatum modo sui ipsius, fius, sed communem, & universi generis humani implicatoriam personam sustinuit.
units.tr: B. From the representative condition of Adam with respect to each individual, since he sustained not merely a private person for himself alone, but a common person, one who embraces the whole human race.

units.la: A. Quî vero hoc perspicuum fiet?
units.tr: A. But how will this become clear?

units.la: B. Ex comparatione Adami cum Christo parallela, instituta ab Apost. Rom. 5.
units.tr: B. From the parallel comparison of Adam with Christ, which the Apostle draws in Romans 5.

units.la: A. Quid ex ista comparatione efficitur?
units.tr: A. What follows from this comparison?

units.la: B. Utrumque scilicet caput & radicem fuisse generi humano, alterum mortis, vitæ alterum; a per Adamum imputatum ab eo genitis peccatum, per Christum ab eo regenitis justitiam. Hinc ille b primus homo, hic secundus dicitur, ac si nemo intervenisset alius; quin & alter c Adamus ob hanc ipsam rationem Ἀνθρωπος appellatur. a Ro. 5.19. b 1 Cor. 15.47. c 1 Cor. 15.45.
units.tr: B. That each of them, namely Adam and Christ, was the head and root of the human race, the one of death and the other of life: through Adam sin is imputed to those born of him, and through Christ righteousness to those born again of him. Hence the one is called the first man and the other the second, as if no other had come between them; and indeed the second Adam is called [ἄνθρωπος] man for this very reason. Rom. 5. 19. 1 Cor. 15. 47. 1 Cor. 15. 45.

units.la: A. Unde demum contagio ista peccati personalis omnes & singulos Adami posteros pervasit?
units.tr: A. From what source, finally, has this personal contagion of sin spread through all and each of Adam's posterity?

units.la: B. Ex traduce, sive per a generationem naturalem; sicut ex pomi sylvestris amputato surculo simile generatur. Sed de modo (ubi satis constat de re) veritatis & modestiæ cultorem lites movere & serere non decet. a Joh. 3.6. Psal. 51.5.
units.tr: B. From traducianism, or through natural generation, just as a shoot cut from a wild apple tree produces a similar one. But concerning the mode (where it is sufficiently clear what the fact is), it does not befit lovers of truth and modesty to stir up and sow quarrels. John 3. 6. Psalm 51. 5.

units.la: A. At istis reclamare videtur lex divina, quæ docet, animam quæ peccat ipsam (non aliam scilicet) morituraм, & quod Filius non portabit iniquitatem Patris, Ezek. 18.20.
units.tr: A. But the divine law seems to contradict this, since it teaches that the soul which sins, that same soul and no other, shall die, and that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Ezek. 18. 20.

units.la: B. Nulla hic est cum dictis istius legis repugnantia, utpote quæ intelligenda est de parentibus proximioribus & privatis, non de primo illo & communi omnium parente, quod ex totius capitis serie & sermone constat.
units.tr: B. There is no contradiction here with the words of that law, since it must be understood of nearer and private parents, not of that first and common parent of all, as is clear from the whole sequence and sense of the chapter.

units.la: A. Habésne quod huic responso adjiciendum velis?
units.tr: A. Have you anything you wish to add to this answer?

units.la: B. Ita, quod nimirum labes ista originalis, quæ omnibus imputatur, omnibus quoque (per generationem scilicet traducta) inhæret, unde non est aliena modò, sed, quoad speciem, sua cuique personalis & propria, quod ex antedictis abundè constiterit.
units.tr: B. Yes: that this original stain, which is imputed to all, also clings to all (namely being transmitted by generation), so that it is not only foreign to each person, but, as to its kind, is each one's own, personal and proper, as has been amply shown from what was said above.

units.la: A. De peccato originali satis : nonne altera est species peccati?
units.tr: A. Enough about original sin: is there not another kind of sin?

units.la: B. Est, nimirum actuale, quod est legis divinæ vel minima transgressio actualis.
units.tr: B. There is: namely actual sin, which is the actual transgression of even the smallest part of the divine law.

units.la: A. Quotuplex est?
units.tr: A. How many kinds are there?

units.la: B. Duplex, vel omissionis, vel commissionis; utrumque rursus cogitati, dicti, facti; quanquam hæc tria peccatum commissionis, magis proprie (quia magis usitato) sonant.
units.tr: B. Two: either of omission or of commission; and each of these again consists of thought, word, or deed; although these three are more properly (because more commonly) called sins of commission.

units.la: Cap. 7. De Novo Fœdere, & Hominis Redemptione seu liberatione per Christum parta.
units.tr: Chapter 7. On the New Covenant, and the redemption or deliverance of man obtained through Christ.

units.la: A. STatum Hominis miserrimum ex peccato ortum dixisti, nulla vero in meliorem transfeundi spes est?
units.tr: A. So you have described the most wretched state of man, arising from sin. Yet is there no hope of passing into a better one?

units.la: B. Imo plurima, virtute Novi (seu Gratiæ) fœderis à Deo cum Homine peccatore initi.
units.tr: B. Indeed there is very much hope, by the power of the New (or Gracious) Covenant, which God made with sinful man.

units.la: A. Quid est istud Fœdus Novum?
units.tr: A. What is this New Covenant?

units.la: B. Est quo Homini lapso, modo a resipiscenti, & in Christum Mediatorem vere b credenti, peccatorum c omnium venia, & d salus æterna, ob e unius Christi merita f gratiosè promittitur.
units.tr: B. It is the covenant by which, to fallen man who is a repentant and who truly b believes in Christ the Mediator, the forgiveness of c all sins and d eternal salvation are graciously promised f, on account of the merits of Christ e alone.

units.la: A. Da veteris illius ante lapsum & novi hujusce Fœderis discrimina?
units.tr: A. What are the differences between that old covenant before the fall and this new one?

units.la: B. Præcipua hæc sunt: 1. in Vetere exigebatur personalis a eaque perfectissima quoad partes & gradus præstanda toti legi obedientia, sub pœna mortis, & in b propria similiter peccantis persona; in Novo sufficit obedientiæ quoad partes omnes c sinceritas, & pœnæ delinquenti debitæ per mediatorem vicarium solutio. a Gal. 3. 10. Deut. 6. 5. b Gen. 2. 17. c Job. 1. 1. Luc. 1: 6. d Is. 53. 5. Gal. 3. 13.
units.tr: B. The chief ones are these. (1) In the Old, a personal obedience was required, and that most perfect in respect of all its parts and degrees, to the whole law, under penalty of death, and to be rendered by the sinning person himself. In the New, sincerity in obedience to all its parts suffices, and the penalty owed by the offender is paid through a substitute, the Mediator. a Gal. 3:10; Deut. 6:5. b Gen. 2:17. c Job 1:1; Luke 1:6. d Isa. 53:5; Gal. 3:13.

units.la: A. Cedo
units.tr: A. Proceed.

units.la: A. Cedò alterum discrimen.
units.tr: A. Let me hear the second difference.

units.la: B. In Novo Fœdere Deus ipse operatur ex beneplacito suo in servandis & facere & velle, conditiones ad salutem requisitas, quod in Veteri ante lapsum fœdere ex usu Liberi arbitrii humani magis pendebat.
units.tr: B. In the New Covenant God himself works, by his own good pleasure, both to will and to do in preserving what is required for salvation. Under the Old Covenant before the fall, this depended more on the exercise of human free will.

units.la: A. Nonne potuit Deus pro infinita sua misericordia sine interventu mediatoris & solutione Debiti peccatorem servare?
units.tr: A. Could not God, in his infinite mercy, have saved the sinner without any intervention of a mediator and without payment of the debt?

units.la: B. Potest Deus quicquid vult, imo, & quæ non vult, sed hoc cum noluisse palam est; unde insuper summæ non minus justitiæ quàm misericordiæ luculentissima ediderit argumenta.
units.tr: B. God can do whatever he wills, indeed even what he does not will; but since it is plain that he has not willed this, he has displayed in addition the most splendid evidence of his justice no less than of his mercy.

units.la: A. Qui sic?
units.tr: A. How so?

units.la: B. Quoniam & totum (hoc pacto) debitum peccatori remisit, & totum à mediatore Christo accepit. Ro. 3. 24, 25.
units.tr: B. Because in this way he both remitted the whole debt to the sinner and received the whole from the Mediator Christ. Rom. 3:24, 25.

units.la: A. An ergo Christus verè satisfecit pro peccatis fidelium?
units.tr: A. Did Christ then truly make satisfaction for the sins of believers?

units.la: B. Prorsus; quod ubique clamat Scriptura; unde dicitur propitiatio, ἱλασμός, ἀντίλυτρον pro peccatis nostris, nec tantum bono nostro, sed vice nostra perpessus. 1 Joh. 2. 2. Mat. 20. 28. 1 Pet. 3. 18. & c. 2. 24. Heb. 9. 28. Is. 53. &c.
units.tr: B. Entirely so; Scripture cries this out everywhere. Hence he is called the propitiation [ἱλασμός] and the ransom [ἀντίλυτρον] for our sins, and he suffered not only for our good but in our place. 1 John 2:2; Matt. 20:28; 1 Pet. 3:18; and ch. 2:24; Heb. 9:28; Isa. 53, etc.

units.la: A. At hoc videtur à justitia remotum, ut aliena quis insons culpa debitam luat pœnam?
units.tr: A. But does it not seem contrary to justice that one who is innocent should pay the penalty owed by another's guilt?

units.la: B. Esset quidem, nisi hoc ultro & nemine ullatenus cognite in se suscipere, idque in Dei gloriam, quod fecit Christus. Heb. 10. 5. ad 10. Joh. 6. 51. 2 Cor. 8. 9. Joh. 17. 4.
units.tr: B. It would indeed be so, were it not that Christ did this of his own accord, taking it upon himself, and that for the glory of God, and without anyone's knowing it in any way. Heb. 10:5ff.; John 6:51; 2 Cor. 8:9; John 17:4.

units.la: A. Sed quomodo Christus poenam peccatori debitam persolvit, cum ea fuit mors aeterna ?
units.tr: A. But how did Christ pay the penalty owed by the sinner, since that penalty was eternal death?

units.la: B. Eandem formaliter poenam minime sustinuit, sed aequivalenter eandem, imo & majorem; idque ob dignitatem personae θεανθρώπου, cujus Patri merito erat charior vita quam universi generis humani, plurisque satisfactio tot & tantis angoribus illius praestita, (quamvis duratione temporanea) quam totius mundi aeterna esset futura.
units.tr: B. He did not undergo the very same penalty formally, but an equivalent one, indeed even a greater one. This was because of the dignity of the person, the God-man [θεανθρώπου], whose life was dearer to the Father, by merit, than the whole human race; and his satisfaction, offered in so many and such great agonies (though temporary in duration), would have been of greater worth than the eternal punishment of the whole world.

units.la: A. Nunquid ergo per unum Christum salutis porta peccatoribus aperitur ?
units.tr: A. Is it therefore through Christ alone that the gate of salvation is opened to sinners?

units.la: B. Ita res est; diserte id testante Scriptura, Joh. 14.6. Act. 4.12. & suffragante ratione: Nam si alius quispiam ad salutem aditus pateret (puta per caecos naturae ductus, aut ex intuendo creaturarum speculo) nulla poterit assignari causa idonea cur in Hominum salutem descenderet à coelo Filius Dei ad Crucem in Terris.
units.tr: B. So it is. Scripture testifies to this plainly, John 14:6; Acts 4:12, and reason agrees. For if some other way of access to salvation lay open (for instance by the blind guidance of nature, or by looking at the mirror of created things), no suitable cause could be assigned why the Son of God should have come down from heaven to the cross on earth for the salvation of men.

units.la: Cap. 8. De officio Christi Mediatorio.
units.tr: Chapter 8. On the Mediatorial Office of Christ.

units.la: A. QUalem oportet esse Mediatorem inter Deum & Hominem?
units.tr: A. What sort of Mediator must there be between God and man?

units.la: B. 1. Ab omni vel minima peccati labecula immunem. Nam frustra pro peccatore medium se Justitiæ Divinæ objiceret peccator. Heb. 7. 26, 27. 2. Utriusque naturæ participem; humanæ, qua scilicet læso numini satisfaciat, magisque Hominem peccatorem affectu sympathetico complectatur Homo; Divinæ, qua satisfactionem atque adeo quicquid est muneris Mediatorii cumulatè adimpleat, eique vim, & meritum affundat. a Heb. 2. 14, 15. b Job. 19. 30. Heb. 10. 14. c Eph. 4. 8, 12. d Rom. 8. 32, 33, 34.
units.tr: B. 1. One free from every, even the smallest, stain of sin. For a sinner would in vain place himself as a go-between before the justice of God. Heb. 7. 26, 27. 2. One who shares both natures: the human, by which he may satisfy the offended majesty and by which man may embrace sinful man with sympathetic feeling; and the divine, by which he may fully accomplish the satisfaction and indeed everything that belongs to the mediatorial office, and may pour into it power and merit. a Heb. 2. 14, 15. b Job. 19. 30. Heb. 10. 14. c Eph. 4. 8, 12. d Rom. 8. 32, 33, 34.

units.la: A. Quotuplex est Christi munus Mediatorium?
units.tr: A. How many-fold is the mediatorial office of Christ?

units.la: B. Triplex; Regium, Sacerdotale, Propheticum. a Mat. 21. 5. b Heb. 6. 20. & alibi passim. c Act. 3. 23.
units.tr: B. Threefold: royal, priestly, and prophetic. a Mat. 21. 5. b Heb. 6. 20. & elsewhere throughout. c Act. 3. 23.

units.la: A. Quæ partes sunt Regii muneris?
units.tr: A. What are the parts of the royal office?

units.la: B. Populo suo leges dare, piis tutelam, privilegia, præmia largiri, & merità impios prosequi vindicta. a Is. 33. 22. Mat. 28. 20. b Joh. 10. 11, 28. c 1 Pet. 2. 9. Apoc. 1. 6. 1 Tim. 4. 8. d Apoc. 22. 12. e Luc. 19. 27.
units.tr: B. To give laws to his people, to bestow protection, privileges and rewards on the godly, and to pursue the wicked with vengeance as they deserve. a Is. 33. 22. Mat. 28. 20. b Joh. 10. 11, 28. c 1 Pet. 2. 9. Apoc. 1. 6. 1 Tim. 4. 8. d Apoc. 22. 12. e Luc. 19. 27.

units.la: A. Quanam ad munus Sacerdotale pertinent?
units.tr: A. What belongs to the priestly office?

units.la: B. In genere duo; 1. seipsum semel pro peccatis offerre victimam Justitiæ Divinæ ex asse satisfactoriam : 2° pro peccatoribus in eum credentibus jugiter apud Patrem intercedere.
units.tr: B. In general two things: 1. once to offer himself as a victim to the justice of God for sins, wholly satisfactory; 2. continually to intercede with the Father for sinners who believe in him.

units.la: A. Quid ergo statuendum est de Sacrificio, quod vocant Missæ, peccatorum (saltem quoad pœnam temporalem) expiatorio?
units.tr: A. What then must be held concerning the sacrifice, which they call the Mass, expiatory of sins (at least as to temporal punishment)?

units.la: B. Blasphemum id esse figmentum Hominum Scripturas non intelligentium: Hæ siquidem nullum tale nobis commendant sacrificium præter sanguinem Christi, qui a solus ablUit peccata. Interim sacrificia Christiana (sensu figurato) agnoscimus, spiritualia scilicet, Eucharistica, & magni illius sacrificii commemorativa, quale est cœna Domini.
units.tr: B. That it is a blasphemous fiction of men who do not understand the Scriptures. For these commend to us no such sacrifice apart from the blood of Christ, which alone cleanses from sins. Meanwhile we acknowledge Christian sacrifices (in a figurative sense), namely spiritual ones, eucharistic ones, and ones commemorating that great sacrifice, such as the Lord's Supper.

units.la: A. Nonne & Sancti in cœlis sunt Mediatores intercessionis?
units.tr: A. Are not also the saints in heaven mediators of intercession?

units.la: B. Nequaquam ; quia a unus sufficit nobis mediator & intercessor Christus, nec ullo vel præcepto vel exemplo in Scripturis propositio ad alios relegamur. a Heb. 7. 25. 1 Tim. 2. 5.
units.tr: B. By no means; because a one mediator and intercessor, Christ, is enough for us, and in Scripture we are not referred to others by any precept or example. a Heb. 7. 25. 1 Tim. 2. 5.

units.la: A. At Sancti in Terris intercedunt pro fratribus suis.
units.tr: A. But the saints on earth intercede for their brothers.

units.la: B. Sane; hoc enim aLex (Divina) charitatis postulat; at vel in genere tantum ( quod & Sanctos in cœlis facere pie credibile est) aut si pro hominibus (eorumque conditionibus) singularibus, intelligendi duntaxat sunt ii, quorum necessitates sibi perspectas habent : Ea vero singularium aliquot cognitio cum Sanctis vita functis b ordinario non competat, uti olim in Terra degentibus (imo {f}imo neque nisi ex revelatione divina competere possit,) inde fit quod Horum preces flagitamus, Illorum ambiendas neutiquam censemus.
units.tr: B. Certainly; for this is required by a (divine) law of charity. But either in general only (which it is also piously credible the saints in heaven do), or, if for individual men and their particular conditions, only those are to be understood who have their needs clearly known to them.
