Yet such knowledge of individuals does not ordinarily belong to those who have departed this life, as it did to those once living on earth (indeed it could not belong to them except by divine revelation). Hence we ask for the prayers of the living, but we by no means think the prayers of the departed are to be sought.

units.la: A. In quo munus suum exercet Christus Propheticum?
units.tr: A. In what does Christ exercise his prophetic office?

units.la: B. Non tantum multa praedicendo, quae aut post evenerunt, aut certò creduntur eventura; verumetiam docendo populum suum, eosque in omnem veritatem ducendo ad salutem necessariam.
units.tr: B. Not only by foretelling many things which have either happened since or are firmly believed to be about to happen, but also by teaching his people and leading them into all truth necessary for salvation.

units.la: A. Quomodo autem id facit?
units.tr: A. But how does he do this?

units.la: B. Intus spiritu, ut causa principali; extra verbo, ut instrumentali, If. 29. 21.
units.tr: B. Inwardly by the Spirit, as the principal cause; outwardly by the Word, as the instrument. Isa. 29. 21.

units.la: Cap. 9, De Fide.
units.tr: Chapter 9, On Faith.

units.la: A. QUotuplex in S. Script. Fides legitur ?
units.tr: A. In how many senses is faith read of in Holy Scripture?

units.la: B. Non uno gaudet significatu ; nam interdum capitur objectivè pro ipsâ Fidei a Doctrina, at sæpius subjectivè, prout est in ipso Credente. a Act. 6.7. Ro. 10.8.
units.tr: B. It does not have one meaning. Sometimes it is taken objectively for the doctrine of the faith itself, but more often subjectively, as it is in the believer. a Act. 6.7. Ro. 10.8.

units.la: A. Sensu autem posteriore quotuplex ?
units.tr: A. In the latter sense, how many kinds are there?

units.la: B. Quadruplicem meminit Scriptura : Fidem seil. a Miraculorum, b Historicam, c Temporanem, & d Justificam. a Mat. 17. 20. 1 Cor. 13.2. b Jac. 2. 19. c Mat. 13. 20, 21. Heb. 6. 4, 5. d Ro. 3. 28.
units.tr: B. Scripture mentions four: (a) miraculous faith, (b) historical faith, (c) temporary faith, and (d) justifying faith. a Mat. 17. 20. 1 Cor. 13.2. b Jac. 2. 19. c Mat. 13. 20, 21. Heb. 6. 4, 5. d Ro. 3. 28.

units.la: A. Quomodo distinguuntur tres ista Fidei species priores à Justifica?
units.tr: A. How are the first three of these kinds of faith distinguished from justifying faith?

units.la: B. Non gradu tantum, sed ipsâ quoque sententiâ.
units.tr: B. Not only by degree, but also by their very meaning.

units.la: A. Unde hoc evincitur?
units.tr: A. How is this proved?

units.la: B. Hinc potissimum, quod diversa habent tum principia, tum subjecta. Nam principium fidei Justificæ est gratia Dei specialis; ad reliquas sufficit generalior, et viribus naturæ magis accommodata. a Eph. 2. 8. Gal. 5.22. 1 Jo. 2. 20. 27. & 6.3.9.
units.tr: B. Chiefly from this, that they have different principles and different subjects. For the principle of justifying faith is the special grace of God; the others need only a more general grace, better suited to the powers of nature. a Eph. 2. 8. Gal. 5.22. 1 Jo. 2. 20. 27. & 6.3.9.

units.la: A. Die subjecta itidem diversa?
units.tr: A. Are the subjects likewise different?

units.la: B. Fidei Justificæ est homo a electus ad vitam, & a natus ex Deo ; reliquarum possunt esse b filii perditionis, c Hypocritæ, (imo fidem Historicam quod attinet) ipsi quoque dDiaboli. aTit. 1.1.
units.tr: B. The subject of justifying faith is a man chosen to life, and born of God; the subjects of the others may be b the sons of perdition, c hypocrites, and (as far as historical faith goes) even d the devils themselves. a Tit. 1.1.

units.la: 1 Jo. 1. 12, 13. b Jo. 17. 12. collat. cum Mat. 10.
units.tr: 1 Jo. 1. 12, 13. b Jo. 17. 12. collated with Mat. 10.

units.la: A. Quid est Fides justificā?
units.tr: A. What is justifying faith?

units.la: B. Habitus animæ humanæ,
units.tr: B. A habit of the human soul.

units.la: A. Quænam est nota Fidei justificantis certissima?
units.tr: A. What is the most certain mark of justifying faith?

units.la: B. Quod purificet cor, & per charitatem agat: a Act. 15. 9. b Gal. 5. 6.
units.tr: B. That it purifies the heart and works through love. a Act. 15. 9. b Gal. 5. 6.

units.la: A. Possuntne Infantes habere fidem?
units.tr: A. Can infants have faith?

units.la: B. Possunt in actu primo eeu radice, non in actu secundo, sive fructu; cum enim verae regenerationis per occultam Sp. S. virtutem capaces esse dubitandum non sit, eosdem quoq; tum fidei, tum omnium eo pertinentium virtutum, in femine, & radice participes fieri nil vetat. Huc accommodetur a Mar. 10. 14. Apoc. 21. 27.
units.tr: B. They can have it in the first act, or as a root, but not in the second act, or as fruit. For since there is no doubt that they are capable of true regeneration through the hidden power of the Holy Spirit, there is nothing to prevent them from also sharing in faith, and in all the virtues belonging to it, in seed and root. Let this be applied to a Mark 10. 14. Rev. 21. 27.

units.la: Cap. 10. De Justificatione & Sanctificatione.
units.tr: Chap. 10. On Justification and Sanctification.

units.la: A. Quid est Justificatio?
units.tr: A. What is justification?

units.la: B. Est actus Dei a judicialis, quo justitia bChristi cuilibet in eum credenti ad salutem cgratis dimputatur. a Ro. 5. 16. & c. 8. 33, 34. b 1 Cor. 1. 30. Phil. 3. 9. c Ro. 3. 24. d Ro. 4. 3. ad v 9.
units.tr: B. It is a judicial act of God, by which the righteousness of Christ is freely imputed to each person who believes in him, for salvation. a Rom. 5:16; ch. 8:33, 34. b 1 Cor. 1:30; Phil. 3:9. c Rom. 3:24. d Rom. 4:3, to v. 9.

units.la: A. Annon ergo justificantur peccatores per justitiam illius infusam seu quovismodo inhaerentem?
units.tr: A. Are sinners then not justified by the righteousness of Christ infused, or inhering in some way?

units.la: B. Nequaquam; (tota enim a Scriptura reclamat) sed per unius Christi justitiam fide apprehensam, & applicatam: consule loca in responsione prox. antecedente. & a Ro. 4. 5. 24. & Ro. 5. 18. Gal. 2. 20. Tit. 3. 4, 5.
units.tr: B. By no means, for the whole of Scripture cries out against this. Rather, they are justified by the righteousness of the one Christ, apprehended by faith and applied to them. Consult the passages in the answer immediately before. Also Rom. 4:5, 24; Rom. 5:18; Gal. 2:20; Titus 3:4, 5.

units.la: A. Quomodo igitur Fides justificare dicitur, cum sit qualitas infusa & inhaerens?
units.tr: A. How then is faith said to justify, when it is an infused and inherent quality?

units.la: B. Non ut causa principalis efficiens, nam ea Deus est; non ut causa meritoria, quae Christus est: sed ut instrumentum quoddam Christi justitiam peccatori applicans. a Ro. 8. 33. b Is. 53. 5. Ro. 5. 19.
units.tr: B. Not as the principal efficient cause, for that is God; not as the meritorious cause, which is Christ; but as a certain instrument applying the righteousness of Christ to the sinner. a Rom. 8:33. b Isa. 53:5; Rom. 5:19.

units.la: A. Quid hic censendum de bonis operibus, quibus justificationem cum fide sociam tribuere videtur S. Jacobus c. 2.
units.tr: A. What is to be held here about good works, to which St. James seems to ascribe justification along with faith, in chapter 2?

units.la: B. Quanquam Scriptura nos sola fide justificari non asserit diserte, & totidem terminis; id tamen locutione prorsus aequipollente, saepies enuntiat; ut cum dicit justificari non operantem, & sine operibus, Ro. 4. 5. Ro. 3. 28.
units.tr: B. Although Scripture does not assert in plain words, and in exactly these terms, that we are justified by faith alone, it nonetheless says so very often in an entirely equivalent way: for example, when it says that a man is justified not working, and without works (Rom. 4:5; Rom. 3:28).

units.la: A. Quomodo ergo intelligendus est S. Jacobus?
units.tr: A. How then is St. James to be understood?

units.la: B. De operibus ut adjunctis fidei justificæ necessariis; non ut ad ipsum (sicut fides est) justificandi actum requisitis; hæc enim (si evangelicè bona) non præcedunt justificandum, sed sequuntur justificatum.
units.tr: B. Of works as necessary accompaniments of living faith, not as things required for the act of justifying itself, as faith is; for these (if they are good in the evangelical sense) do not precede the justified, but follow the justified.

units.la: A. An ergo nulla datur justificatio ante fidem?
units.tr: A. Is there then no justification before faith?

units.la: B. Nulla prorsus in a foro Conscientiæ; imò nec in foro Dei b actualis & completa; datur tamen in c decreto divino, & quæ virtualis appellatur in capite d Christo. a Ro. 5. 1. b Heb. 11. 6. c Eph. 1. 11, 12, 13. d Is. 50. 8.
units.tr: B. None at all in the forum of conscience; nor indeed in the forum of God is it actual and complete; yet it is given in the divine decree, and in Christ it is called virtual. a Rom. 5:1. b Heb. 11:6. c Eph. 1:11, 12, 13. d Isa. 50:8.

units.la: A. Num justificatio simul & semel peragitur?
units.tr: A. Is justification accomplished at once and once for all?

units.la: B. Ita, sed quoad gradus (sic enim omnibus & omni quoque tempore e eadem est) non vero quoad ejus sive sensum, sive durationem; utpote peccatori credenti, & resipiscenti continenter repetita. e Ez. 18. 22. f Ro. 3. 25.
units.tr: B. Yes, as to its degree (for it is the same for all and at all times), but not as to its sense or its duration, since it is continually repeated for the sinner who believes and repents. e Ezek. 18:22. f Rom. 3:25.

units.la: A. An denique est Homini lapso sub lege eadem, quæ sub Evangelio justificatio?
units.tr: A. Finally, is justification the same for a fallen man under the law as it is under the Gospel?

units.la: B. Eadem, per fidem scil. in g Christum mediatorem (utrobique communem) sub lege exhibendum, sub Evangelio exhibitum. g Heb. 10. ad v. 15. & c. 11. per tot. & c. 4. 2. 1 Cor. 10. 3, 4. & alibi passim.
units.tr: B. It is the same, namely through faith in Christ the mediator (common to both), to be exhibited under the law, and exhibited under the Gospel. g Heb. 10, from v. 15; and ch. 11 throughout; and ch. 4:2; 1 Cor. 10:3, 4; and elsewhere throughout.

units.la: A. Itaque promissionibus spiritualibus non carnere fideles ante incarnatum Christum?
units.tr: A. So the faithful before the incarnate Christ did not lack the spiritual promises?

units.la: B. Nullatenus: nam sic aut vana aut cæca admodum fuisset illorum fides: quin & discrte contrarium asserit Apost. Heb. 11. 13. ad 17.
units.tr: B. By no means, for otherwise their faith would have been quite empty or blind. Indeed the Apostle expressly asserts the contrary: Heb. 11:13 to 17.

units.la: A. Potestne instantia aliqua V. T. res clarior fieri?
units.tr: A. Can some instance from the Old Testament be made clearer?

units.la: B. Omnino, idque ex verbis ipsis pacti cum Abrahamo foederis, Gen. 17. 7. Ero tibi Deus & semini tuo.
units.tr: B. Certainly, and that from the very words of the covenant made with Abraham, Gen. 17:7: "I will be a God to you and to your seed."

units.la: A. Quid inde conficitur?
units.tr: A. What follows from this?

units.la: B. Promissiones factas esse Patribus & fidelibus ante Christum plusquam terrenas: imo Christum ipsum, (qui promissionum omnium nucleus est) eis promissum & praedicatum fuisse constat, ex Gal. 3. 8, 14, 16, 17, 18.
units.tr: B. It is established that the promises made to the Fathers and the faithful before Christ were more than earthly; indeed it is clear that Christ himself, who is the kernel of all the promises, was promised and preached to them, from Gal. 3:8, 14, 16, 17, 18.

units.la: A. Quid est Sanctificatio?
units.tr: A. What is sanctification?

units.la: B. Est actio Dei gratuita, qua peccatorem jam h justificatum, peccati i omnis dominio, per k Spiritum suum l gradatim liberat; eumque studio constante bonorum operum inflammat. h Ro. 8. 1, 2. Heb. 11. per totum. i Ro. 6. 14. k Ro. 8. passim, l Phil. 3. 14.
units.tr: B. It is the free action of God by which he gradually frees the sinner, already justified, from the dominion of every sin, through his Spirit, and inflames him with a constant zeal for good works. h Rom. 8:1, 2; Heb. 11 throughout. i Rom. 6:14. k Rom. 8 throughout. l Phil. 3:14.

units.la: A. In quo discrepat sanctificatio a justificatione?
units.tr: A. In what does sanctification differ from justification?

units.la: B. In tribus potissimum, (si strictius prout in descriptione exhibetur, accepta)
units.tr: B. Chiefly in three respects (if it is taken more strictly, as it is set out in the description):

units.la: 1. quod sit natura posterior justificatione, (nam tempore coincidunt)
units.tr: 1. that it is posterior in nature to justification (for in time they coincide);

units.la: 2. quod sit qualitas animae Credentis realiter inhaerens, eamque modo reali & absoluto afficiens.
units.tr: 2. that it is a quality really inhering in the soul of the believer, and affects it in a real and absolute manner;

units.la: 3. quod per gradus absolvitur, Phil. 3. 12, 14. 2 Pet. 3. 18.
units.tr: 3. that it is carried through by degrees. Phil. 3:12, 14; 2 Pet. 3:18.

units.la: A. Quam ad regulam exigendum est huius sanctificationis exercitium?
units.tr: A. By what rule is the practice of this sanctification to be measured?

units.la: B. Ad unum Dei verbum in Scripturis consignatum, praecipue ad Decalogum Sanctimoniae normam summariam.
units.tr: B. By the one Word of God set down in the Scriptures, especially by the Decalogue, the summary standard of holiness.

units.la: Cap. II. De Decalogo.
units.tr: Chapter 2. On the Decalogue.

units.la: A. Num Decalogus Christianos ex æquo cum Judæis obligat?
units.tr: A. Does the Decalogue bind Christians equally with the Jews?

units.la: B. Omnino: Lex enim naturæ (ceu moralis) quam exhibet est omnium hominum (idque æternum) obligatoria; quod idem constat ex Christi & Apostolorum testimonio, qui ad legem in Decalogo comprehensam, ut sanctitatis regulam omnes amandant: ut Mat.15.3,4. Lu. 10.26. Ja. 2.8.11.
units.tr: B. Certainly. The law of nature, insofar as it is moral, which the Decalogue sets forth, binds all men, and binds them eternally. Christ and the Apostles bear the same witness, since all of them refer to the law comprehended in the Decalogue as the rule of holiness: as in Mat.15.3,4. Lu. 10.26. Ja. 2.8.11.

units.la: A. Quomodo distribuitur Decalogus?
units.tr: A. How is the Decalogue divided?

units.la: B. In binas (quas vocant) Tabulas, ceu mandata magna (generalia) ut appellat Christus, Mat. 22. 38, 39, 40.
units.tr: B. Into two so-called Tables, or the great commandments (general ones), as Christ calls them, Mat. 22. 38, 39, 40.

units.la: A. Iste autem Tabulæ quomodo distinguuntur?
units.tr: A. How are these Tables distinguished?

units.la: B. Prior (quæ 4. Ia continet præcepta) Deum immediate respicit; altera proximum, vel Deum, mediante proximo.
units.tr: B. The first, which contains the first four precepts, looks directly to God; the second looks to our neighbour, or to God through our neighbour.

units.la: A. Quæ sunt regulæ ad interpretandum Decalogum observatu digniores?
units.tr: A. What rules for interpreting the Decalogue are most worth observing?

units.la: B. Istæ tres:
units.tr: B. These three:

units.la: 1a. Præceptum omne negativum, oppositas exigit virtutes: exempla vid. 1Cor. 15. 34. Eph. 4. 28. If. 58. 4. ad 8. Rom. 12. 2. &c.
units.tr: (1) Every negative precept requires the opposite virtues. Examples: 1Cor. 15. 34. Eph. 4. 28. Is. 58. 4 to 8. Rom. 12. 2, etc.

units.la: 2a. Mandatum generale omnes includit species, imo & occasiones quaslibet non pure accidentarias, irritamenta, atque adeo quaecunque eo conducentia adminicula.
units.tr: (2) A general command includes all its species, and indeed all occasions that are not purely accidental, all incentives, and therefore whatever aids conduce to it.

units.la: 3a Praecepta affirmantia obligant semper; negativa, insuper ad semper: v. g. semper tenemur dare pauperibus, sed non dare semper; quod si nullo vitae, totius momento eos opprimamus, violatur lex negativa, quae id severe prohibet.
units.tr: (3) Affirmative precepts bind always; negative precepts bind, in addition, for always. For example, we are always bound to give to the poor, but we are not bound to give always. If at any moment of our life we oppress them, we violate the negative law, which strictly forbids this.

units.la: A. Ecquid legi in Decalogo comprehensa, novum aliquod praeceptum substantiale Christus attexuit?
units.tr: A. Did Christ add any new substantive precept to the law comprehended in the Decalogue?

units.la: B. Prorsus nullum, quia sic lex divina non esset perfecta, totum continens officii humani, contra Psal. 19. 7. imo perfectio (& hoc ipso nomine) ei tribuitur, nullis finibus circumscripta, Psal. 119. 96. Praeterea sequeretur quod si quis totam legem cumulate adimpleret, nondum tamen officii sui partes omnes percurreret, quia peragendae restarent aliae a Christo Domino adscriptae; nec posset consequenter introire vitam, reclamante totius Scripturae suffragio.
units.tr: B. Absolutely none. Otherwise the divine law would not be perfect, containing the whole of human duty, contrary to Psal. 19. 7. Indeed it is ascribed perfection, and by this very name, being bounded by no limits, Psal. 119. 96. Moreover, it would follow that if anyone fulfilled the whole law abundantly, he would still not have gone through all the parts of his duty, since other parts, assigned by Christ the Lord, would remain to be performed; and consequently he could not enter into life, the whole witness of Scripture opposing this.

units.la: A. Quid ergo hac in re Christum praestitisse censendum est?
units.tr: A. What, then, must we judge Christ to have accomplished in this matter?

units.la: B. Veteri nimirum legi lucem attulisse novam, nova (nec satis unquam miranda) impositae hominibus Christianis obsequii vincula.
units.tr: B. Surely that he brought new light to the old law, and new bonds of obedience (never sufficiently to be admired) laid upon Christian men.

units.la: A. At pactum praestantius, & promissa praestantiora legimus: Heb. 8. 9.
units.tr: A. But we read of a better covenant and better promises: Heb. 8. 9.

units.la: B. Foedus Evangelicum & gratiae, esse operum foederi praestantius, in confesso est apud omnes: sed cum foedus illud gratiae sit duplex, vel typicum scilicet, vel spirituale: prioti videtur hic opponi posterius, quod cum promissa spiritualia exhibeat tum uberius multo, tum dilucidius, foedus ipsum praestantius, & promissis praestantioribus stabilitum dicatur. Vide Heb. 8. 11.
units.tr: B. That the Evangelical covenant of grace is more excellent than the covenant of works is admitted by all. But since that covenant of grace is twofold, either typical, namely, or spiritual, the latter seems here to be set against the former. Since it presents spiritual promises both far more abundantly and far more clearly, it is said to be the more excellent covenant itself, and established on better promises. See Heb. 8. 11.

units.la: A. Quid existimandum est de operibus (quae vocant) supererogationis, quaeque meriti esse maximi dicuntur, neque tamen intra ambitum Decalogi conclusa qualia somniant Pontificii, sua caelibatus, obedientiae, & paupertatis spontanea vota, quibus veluti quartum adjecerunt Jesuita sibi proprium, viz. missionis?
units.tr: A. What is to be thought of the so-called works of supererogation, which are said to have the greatest merit, and yet are not contained within the compass of the Decalogue? The Papists dream of such things: their vows of celibacy, of obedience and of voluntary poverty, to which, as a fourth, they have added the vow of mission, which is peculiar to the Jesuits.

units.la: B. Fieri non potest ut opus ullum morale extra legem moralem (nedum supra) collocetur, nam latum mandatum tuum nimis, Psal. 119. 96. rejiciendaque itaque consilia illa horum sensu Evangelica dicta, quae ut aiunt, suadent tantum, nullo modo praecipiunt: nam si suadent ad bonum, omne bonum in lege bona & perfecta, vel in specie, vel in genere, vel expresse, vel implicite continetur. g Mat. 14. 21. h Deut. 6. 5. collat. cum Mat. 22. 37.
units.tr: B. It cannot be that any moral work is placed outside the moral law, much less above it, for "your commandment is exceedingly broad," Psal. 119. 96. Those counsels, which are called evangelical sayings and which, as they say, only advise and in no way command, must therefore be rejected. For if they advise toward good, every good is contained in the good and perfect law, either in species, or in genus, or expressly, or implicitly. g Mat. 14. 21. h Deut. 6. 5, compared with Mat. 22. 37.

units.la: A. Quid vero de votis istis censendum?
units.tr: A. But what is to be thought of those vows?

units.la: B. Omnia rationi & Scripturae adversari: nam quod ad votum paupertatis attinet, id erga Deum i ingratitudinem, erga b se & proximum charitatis defectum arguit. Votum caelibatus pugnat contra remedium incontinentiæ à Deo omnibus ex æquo indultum, & promissione divina caret. Votum obedientiæ & missionis, prout à Pontificiis describitur, est obedire Hominibus magis quam Deo: Pro. 30. 8, 9. Pro. 3. 10. 16. 1 Tim. 5. 8. 1 Cor. 7, 9. Heb. 13. 4.
units.tr: B. They are all opposed to reason and Scripture. As for the vow of poverty, it argues ingratitude toward God and a lack of charity toward oneself and one's neighbour. The vow of celibacy fights against the remedy for incontinence granted by God equally to all, and it lacks any divine promise. The vow of obedience and mission, as the Papists describe it, means to obey men rather than God: Pro. 30. 8, 9. Pro. 3. 10. 16. 1 Tim. 5. 8. 1 Cor. 7, 9. Heb. 13. 4.

units.la: Cap. 12. De Sabbatho
units.tr: Chapter 12. On the Sabbath

units.la: {A}Cum Sabbatum a Deo ipso esse insti-tutum, imo & in Arca fœderis una cum reliquo Decalogo præceptum de pia atque inviolanda ejus observantia depositum, variis insuper & , & , utrum tamen juris naturalis (immutabilis) an positivi censendum erit?
units.tr: {A}Since the Sabbath was instituted by God himself, and indeed the precept of its pious and inviolable observance was deposited in the Ark of the covenant along with the rest of the Decalogue, and [variis insuper & , &] by various other [...] and [...], it must nevertheless be asked whether it is to be considered a matter of natural (immutable) law or of positive law.

units.la: B. Est juris naturalis quoad substantiam præcepti, i. e. cultum Dei solennem, & publicum, eumque stato aliquo tempore exhibendum (hoc enim ratio naturalis dictabit) est juris positivi divini quoad circumstantiam, ut scilicet hac hora aut die celebretur.
units.tr: B. It is of natural law as to the substance of the precept, that is, that God be worshipped solemnly and publicly and that this be done at some fixed time (for natural reason itself dictates this). It is of positive divine law as to the circumstance, namely that it be celebrated at this hour or on this day.

units.la: A. Quando primum Deus sanctificavit Sabbatum?
units.tr: A. When did God first sanctify the Sabbath?

units.la: B. Statim à finita mundi creatione, die nimirum septima, quanquam variis populi Dei migrationibus, & servitute potissimum Ægyptiaca ita neglectum, ut nullum ejus celebrandi ante Mosen discrtum occurrat exemplum.
units.tr: B. Immediately after the completion of the creation of the world, namely on the seventh day, although during the various migrations of God's people, and especially under the Egyptian servitude, it was so neglected that no distinct example of its observance before Moses occurs.

units.la: A. Verum si ab orbe condito obtinuit Sabbati obligatio, cur dicitur signum datum Israelitis? Exod. 31. 13.
units.tr: A. But if the obligation of the Sabbath has held since the foundation of the world, why is it said to have been given as a sign to the Israelites? Exod. 31. 13.

units.la: B. Non quod tum primum esset institutum, sed restitutum (ceu de novo repetitum) & signum dicitur, non quasi nullam ante haberet significationem, sed quod Israel, ex parte tum obligationis, tum materiae, novam, Exod. 31. 17. collat. cum v. 3. Deut. 5. 15.
units.tr: B. Not because it was then first instituted, but because it was restored (as if repeated anew), and it is called a sign not as though it had no significance before, but because Israel, in part both of the obligation and of the matter, received it in a new way. Exod. 31. 17, compared with v. 3, Deut. 5. 15.

units.la: A. Cur mutatum est Sabbatum Christianum a die 7o hebdomadis in primum?
units.tr: A. Why was the Christian Sabbath changed from the seventh day of the week to the first?

units.la: B. In memoriam resurrectionis die Dominica; unde & dies dicitur Dominicus, Apoc. 1. 10.
units.tr: B. In memory of the resurrection, on the Lord's day; whence the day is also called the Lord's Day, Apoc. 1. 10.

units.la: B: Sed qua authoritate facta est dici mutatio?
units.tr: B. But by what authority was this change made?

units.la: A. Omnino videtur quod divina, i. e. vel Christo ipso a mortuis excitato, vel Apostolis, monente Spiritu sancto, ita decernentibus.
units.tr: A. It seems altogether to be divine, that is, either by Christ himself raised from the dead, or by the Apostles, so decreeing under the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: A. Quam hujus rationem affers?
units.tr: A. What reason do you give for this?

units.la: B. ro, quod nonnulla mutationis istius indicia verisimilia habeantur in Scriptura. 2o, quia a tempore Apostolorum praxis ea passim invaluit in Ecclesia. Act. 20. 7. 1 Cor. 16. 2.
units.tr: B. (1) That some probable indications of this change are found in Scripture; (2) that from the time of the Apostles this practice widely prevailed in the Church. Acts 20. 7; 1 Cor. 16. 2.

units.la: A. Num dies integer debetur Sabbato sanctificando?
units.tr: A. Is the whole day owed to the sanctification of the Sabbath?

units.la: B. Nullam diei partem exceptam regimus, qua licet aliquid agere (citra casum aut necessitatis, aut charitatis) quod solennem Sabbati sanctificationem impediat. Mat. 12. 11.
units.tr: B. We exclude no part of the day in which it is lawful to do something (apart from a case of necessity or of charity) that would hinder the solemn sanctification of the Sabbath. Matt. 12. 11.

units.la: A. Ergo tenentur Christiani ad diei Dominicae, ac Judaei ad sui Sabbati observantiam?
units.tr: A. Therefore Christians are bound to observe the Lord's day, and Jews their own Sabbath?

units.la: B. Quoad opera pietatis & cultus Divini tenentur, etsi non quoad rigorem circumstantiarum populo peculiarium. Vide Num. 15. a v. 32. ad 37.
units.tr: B. They are bound as to the works of piety and the worship of God, though not as to the strictness of circumstances peculiar to the people. See Num. 15, from v. 32 to 37.

units.la: Cap. 13. De obedientia in Quinto Decalogo præcepto mandatâ.
units.tr: Chapter 13. On the obedience enjoined in the Fifth Commandment.

units.la: A. QUinam Patris & Matris nomine in isto præcepto intelliguntur?
units.tr: A. In what sense are the father and mother understood in this commandment?

units.la: B. Non ii tantum, à quibus progeniti sumus, sed qui nobis legitimè præsunt, aut superiores jure audiunt, in statu sive Oeconomico, sive Politico, sive denum Ecclesiastico.
units.tr: B. Not only those from whom we have been begotten, but those who lawfully preside over us, or whom we are rightly bound to obey as superiors, in the household, in the civil state, or finally in the Church.

units.la: A. Quis autem iis debetur honos?
units.tr: A. What honour, moreover, is owed to them?

units.la: B. Non illius externæ modo in vultu, gestu, dictisque reverentiæ, imò neque debiti personarum intus æstimii, sed prompti quoque & fidelis obsequii illorum licitis quibuscunque mandatis & sanctionibus deferendi.
units.tr: B. Not merely that outward reverence shown in look, gesture and words, nor even the inward esteem due to their persons, but also a ready and faithful obedience, rendered to all their lawful commands and decrees.

units.la: A. Cum vero circa obedientiam in hoc præcepto stat uminatæ materiam periculosissimè (idque à non unius Sectæ Hominibus) erretur, primum de obedientia in universum quæro, utrum cæcam esse par sit?
units.tr: A. Since, however, the matter of obedience in this commandment is very dangerously mishandled (and by people of more than one sect), I ask first about obedience in general: whether it ought to be blind?

units.la: B. Per cæcam obedientiam opinor te intelligere Jesuiticam illam, quam superioribus suis (Generali præsertim & Pontifici) activè præstandam volunt, non tantum non assentiente, sed pertinaciter reclamante proprio obsequentis judicio. Ea non video, quî sit aut Religioni aut Rationi consentanea.
units.tr: B. By "blind obedience" I suppose you mean that Jesuit obedience, which they wish to be rendered actively to superiors (especially the General and the Pope), not merely without assent, but with the subject's own judgment stubbornly objecting. I do not see how it agrees with either religion or reason.

units.la: A. Cur autem primò non Religioni?
units.tr: A. Why, then, do you say first that it does not agree with religion?

units.la: B. Quoniam illa diserte præcipit cavere ne seducamur, ne cuilibet spiritui non ante explorato fidem habeamus, ut omnia ad examen revocemus, nec nisi bonum quicquam retineamus ; monet denique quod quicquid non ex fide est, peccatum est, & si cæcus cæcum duxerit, utrumbo in foveam decident; quæ singula, & id genus complura alia cæcæ isti obedientiæ è diametro adversantur.
units.tr: B. Because religion expressly commands us to beware of being led astray, not to give credence to every spirit before it has been tested, to bring everything to the test, and to keep only what is good. Finally it warns that whatever is not of faith is sin, and that if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit. Each of these, and many others of this kind, is diametrically opposed to that blind obedience.

units.la: A. Cur secundò talem obedientiam à ratione alienam censes?
units.tr: A. Why do you judge such obedience also foreign to reason?

units.la: B. Quoniam eâ quis facit, quod Homo sobrius in re multò leviori minime faceret ; vult enim oculis sibi alienis videri viam æternæ vitæ, non suis, aliena fide credere, non sua; quod est oculos sibi proprios habere frustra, non obedire ut hominem, Deo, sed creaturæ, ut jumentum domino, non ipsum obedientem credere, sed alium; consequenter, videre & non videre, credere & non credere ; ἀσύγκριτα omnia.
units.tr: B. Because by it a man does what a sober person would not do even in a much smaller matter. For he wishes to see the way of eternal life with other men's eyes, not his own, and to believe with another's faith, not his own. This is to have eyes of one's own in vain; it is to obey not as a man obeys God, but as a creature obeys its master, as a beast of burden obeys its driver; it is not to believe oneself, the one obeying, but someone else. Consequently it is to see and not to see, to believe and not to believe: all things [ἀσύγκριτα] incongruous.

units.la: A. Verum in hac cæca obedientia fortasse excipiendum est peccatum?
units.tr: A. But perhaps in this blind obedience sin should be excepted?

units.la: B. Verbo excipi potest, re non excipitur : sic enim vel apparet superiori esse peccatum, vel subdito : non superiori ; Nam supponendus est ille faciendum non injungere peccatum : non subdito, utpote cui jam eruti sunt oculi, nec debet ille (si maxime posset) peccatum pronunciare, quod tale superiori non videtur.
units.tr: B. It can be excepted in words, but in fact it is not excepted. For in that case it would appear to be sin either for the superior or for the subject. Not for the superior, since he must be assumed not to command sin; not for the subject, since his eyes have already been put out, and he ought not (even if he could) to pronounce something a sin which does not seem so to the superior.

units.la: A. Ergo liberum relinquis subdito mandato susuperioris examinandi facultatem?
units.tr: A. So you leave to the subject the freedom to examine his superior's command?

units.la: B. Ita, privatâ quidem diiscretionis judicio, non eam tamen vagam, sed debitis finibus circumscriptam.
units.tr: B. Yes, by the private judgment of discretion; not, however, a vague one, but one confined within its proper limits.

units.la: A. Quinam verò isti sunt fines?
units.tr: A. What, then, are those limits?

units.la: B. Hi sunt praecipui: 1°, ut ne id anxie quis faciat, nisi in materia graviori, & ubi Deus in verbo suo contrarium praecepisse videatur, 2°, ut sobrie & modestè, non petulanter, animoque ad discendum, non ad cavillandum parato aut detrectet aut disputet obsequium. 3°, ut sibi uni examinet, non alius, nisi quorum animarum tutelam habet.
units.tr: B. The principal ones are these: (1) that a person should do this anxiously only in a weightier matter, and where God seems to have commanded the contrary in his word; (2) that he should refuse or dispute obedience soberly and modestly, not wantonly, and with a mind ready to learn, not to cavil; (3) that he should examine for himself alone, and not for others, unless he has the care of their souls.

units.la: A. Pergamus ad obedientiam ca(sum) in specie, & primo in statu Oeconomico; post nuptias liberi, vel inito conjugio, vel alio quovis modo e potestate parentum, ipsis nolentibus, exire?
units.tr: A. Let us go on to the case in particular within the household state. Once married, or by entering a marriage, or in some other way, children leave their parents' authority against the parents' will?

units.la: B. De liberis minorennibus & nondum per aetatem emancipatis nulla difficultas est. Horum enim conjugia quod attinet, sine parentum consensu peragenda omnino non esse S. Scrip. cum dictis, tum piorum exemplis abunde demonstravit: quod etiam ad alia vitae genera per analogiam ex aequo trahendum ratio dictabit, quin & jus naturae una cum civili hoc idem constituat.
units.tr: B. There is no difficulty concerning minor children who have not yet been emancipated by age. For Holy Scripture has amply shown, both by its sayings and by the examples of the godly, that their marriages must by no means be contracted without the parents' consent. Reason will also dictate that the same applies by analogy to other kinds of life, and indeed the law of nature, together with civil law, establishes the same.

units.la: A. Quid si pater consenserit, mater recusaverit?
units.tr: A. What if the father has consented but the mother has refused?

units.la: B. Si in eundem consensum flecti non potest mater ( debitis & mora & medius quibuscunque adhibitis ) suffecerit mariti consensus, qui est caput mulieris,& penes quem patriae potefitatis multo potiorem residere partem omnes agnoscunt.
units.tr: B. If the mother cannot be brought to the same consent (after due delay and all suitable means have been used), the consent of the husband suffices, since he is the head of the wife, and everyone acknowledges that the far greater part of paternal power rests with him.

units.la: A. Si Parentum utrique tum a liberis (ea qua par est reverentia ) tum a communibus amicis sapientibus rogati pertinaciter abnuerint, quid hoc in casu faciendum censes ?
units.tr: A. If both parents persistently refuse, although they have been asked by their children (with the reverence that is fitting) and by common wise friends, what do you think should be done in this case?

units.la: B. Tali conjugio ante mutatam parentum voluntatem omnino abstinendum judico : dato enim quod hoc pro suo tantum imperio & mera animi libidine parentes fecerint, in eo quidem hi graviter peccant, morosis tamen & iniquioribus obsequium debetur non secus ac moderatis & bonis, 1 Pet. 2. 18. ( Quod enim de fervis dicit Apoft. liberis quoque in praesente casu ex aequo accommodandum est. )
units.tr: B. I judge that one must altogether refrain from such a marriage until the parents change their will. For even if the parents have acted merely from their own authority and a bare whim of mind, they sin gravely in this. Nevertheless, obedience is owed to the difficult and the unjust no less than to the moderate and the good: 1 Pet. 2. 18. (What the Apostle says of servants must equally be applied to children in the present case.)

units.la: A. Atqui poterunt hoc pacto Parentes nuptias quascunque liberis suis interdicere, & consequenter ad celibatum perpetuum obligare ?
units.tr: A. But by this method parents will be able to forbid their children any marriage whatsoever, and consequently bind them to perpetual celibacy?

units.la: B. Non sequitur, quia aliud est non huic nubere, aliud nulli; nec potest authoritas humana praejudicare divina, quae a peccati remedium inftituit conjugium. a 1 Cor. 7. 2.
units.tr: B. It does not follow, because it is one thing not to marry this person, and another not to marry no one. Nor can human authority prejudice divine authority, which instituted marriage as the remedy against sin: 1 Cor. 7. 2.

units.la: A. Quid tamen fi adhuc perfient in sententia pa-rentes?
units.tr: A. But what if the parents still persist in their opinion?

units.la: B. Omnino provocandum est ad sententiam Principis (five supremi magistratus) cujus est providere, ut ita fingsuli utantur potestate sua, ne quid inde Respublica detrimenti capiat.
units.tr: B. One must altogether appeal to the judgment of the Prince (or the supreme magistrate), whose duty it is to see that each person uses his power in such a way that the commonwealth suffers no harm from it.

units.la: A. De liberis emancipatis & majorennibus quid quid in præsente negotio statuendum?
units.tr: A. What must be decided in the present matter concerning emancipated and adult children?

units.la: B. Debitam semper parentibus exhibendam esse reverentiam, eorum (quoad fieri potest) consiliis auscultando, ubi vero ad maturam ætatem pervenerint, neque amplius pars sunt familiæ paternæ (idque cum parentum ipsorum consensu) major illis connubiorum a libertas concedenda videtur, ita ut invitis etiam parentibus ea possint contrahere, utpote sui jam juris facti, Vid. Gen. 41.45.
units.tr: B. Due reverence must always be shown to parents, listening to their counsel (as far as it can be done). But when children have reached mature age and are no longer part of the paternal household (and this with the parents' own consent), a greater freedom of marriage seems to be granted to them, so that they may contract marriage even against the parents' will, since they have now become their own masters. See Gen. 41.45.

units.la: A. De obedientia in statu Oeconomico ista suffecerint; de ea quæ rectoribus Ecclesiasticis debetur nonnulla cap. seq. dicemus. Pergamus ad regimen civile; & primo, quam habet Princeps in Clerum potestatem?
units.tr: A. Let this suffice concerning obedience in the household state; we will speak of what is owed to ecclesiastical rulers in the following chapter. Let us go on to civil government. First, what power does the Prince have over the clergy?

units.la: B. Supremam in Terris habet, hoc est in foro externo, non autem interno.
units.tr: B. He has supreme power on earth, that is, in the external forum, but not in the internal.

units.la: A. Id amplius explicandum velim.
units.tr: A. I would like this explained further.

units.la: B. Non in foro interno, utpote cui non sunt datæ claves regni cœlorum, sive per prædicationem verbi, sive per administrationem Sacramentorum, ceu demum per delinquentium excommunicationem, aut pœnitentium absolutionem, aut a alium quemcunque actum pure Ecclesiasticum. a 2 Chron. 26.16.
units.tr: B. Not in the internal forum, since the keys of the kingdom of heaven have not been given to him, whether through the preaching of the Word, or through the administration of the Sacraments, or finally through the excommunication of offenders, the absolution of penitents, or any other purely ecclesiastical act. 2 Chron. 26.16.

units.la: A. Qualis autem est ea, quam dixisti, potestas suprema in foro externo?
units.tr: A. What, then, is that supreme power in the external forum which you mentioned?

units.la: B. Providendi scilicet, ut quod sui est muneris in religionis negotio a quisque faciat, & b gladio civili in contumaces animadvertendi. a 2 Chron. 19.8. ad finem, & c. 29.5. 11.27, 30. & c. 30.5. & c. 31.2. ad 6. & c. 35. ad 7.
units.tr: B. Namely, that of seeing to it that each person performs what belongs to his office in religious affairs, and that the disobedient are punished with the civil sword. 2 Chron. 19.8 to the end; and ch. 29.5, 11, 27, 30; ch. 30.5; ch. 31.2 to 6; and ch. 35 to 7.

units.la: videsis Artic. Relig. Anglic. 37. Ro. 13. 4.
units.tr: See Article 37 of the Articles of Religion of the Church of England. Rom. 13.4.

units.la: A. Licétne subditis, ullo stimulante pratexta, arma sumere, adversus Principem ?
units.tr: A. Is it lawful for subjects, under any pretext whatsoever, to take up arms against the Prince?

units.la: B. Non licet; quia tum verbo Dei, tum piorum omnium exemplis (sub Lege, sub Evangelio) palam repugnat.
units.tr: B. It is not lawful, because it openly contradicts both the Word of God and the examples of all the godly (under the Law and under the Gospel).

units.la: A. Quae profers exempla piorum sub lege?
units.tr: A. What examples of the godly under the Law do you offer?

units.la: B. Davidis, qui licet Sauli divinitus esset designatus successor, tamen armato illius odio, quamvis maximè immerito, non armis adversis, sed fuga, bonitate, patientia obsistendum duxit. Vid.
units.tr: B. That of David, who, although he had been divinely designated as Saul's successor, nevertheless judged that, against Saul's hatred, however very undeserved, he should resist not with hostile arms but with flight, goodness and patience. See 1 Sam. from ch. 18 to ch. 17, especially ch. 24.

units.la: 1 Sam. à c. 18. ad c. 17. præcipuè c. 24.
units.tr: 1 Sam. from ch. 18 to ch. 17, especially ch. 24.

units.la: A. Nunquid his habes alia, quae adjicias exempla aurante legè?
units.tr: A. Do you have other examples, besides these, that you could add from the law of the Gospel?

units.la: B. Imò Prophetarum ad unum omnium, qui pessimorum regum temporibus vixerunt, eosque Dei nomine severissime increpabant, nunquam illi ad rebellionem subditos vel verbo follicitabant.
units.tr: B. Indeed, of all the Prophets, who lived in the times of the most wicked kings and rebuked them most severely in God's name, not one ever urged his subjects to rebellion, even by word.

units.la: A. Exempla quaedam habes sub Evangelio ?
units.tr: A. Do you have some examples under the Gospel?

units.la: B. Innumera; ipsius nimirum Christi dum in Terris versaretur, ejusque Apostolorum, atque adeo omnium priscae Ecclesiae Christianorum ad usque tyrannidis Pontificia tempora, qui gravissimis regum suorum persecutionibus miserè vexati, nunquam tamen ad alia quam precum & lacrymarum arma convolarunt; quod nulli non testantur Apologistae Christiani.
units.tr: B. Countless ones: those of Christ himself while he dwelt on earth, of his Apostles, and indeed of all the Christians of the early Church down to the times of Papal tyranny, who, cruelly harassed by the most grievous persecutions from their rulers, never flew to any weapons other than prayers and tears; as all the Christian Apologists bear witness.

units.la: A. Verum illis fortasse defuit rebellandi non animus, sed facultas.
units.tr: A. But perhaps they lacked the ability to rebel, though not the will.

units.la: B. Imo gravis haec esset eáque crassissima in
units.tr: B. Indeed, this would be a serious and, moreover, a very gross slander against the piety of those heroes,

units.la: Heroum istorum pietatem calumnia, quam & ratio ipsa, & universæ Ecclesiæ primævæ Hiltoria nullo refellit negotio.
units.tr: which neither reason itself nor the whole history of the primitive Church refutes with any difficulty.

units.la: A. Quomodo autem Ratio?
units.tr: A. But how does reason refute it?

units.la: B. Quia cum tantus ubique effet Christianorum numerus, ut a omnia implerent loca, eorumque multi non essent infimi ordinis homunculi, potuissent verisimiliter, modo id ipsis visum suisset, in majorem se libertatem armis afferere. a Tertull. Apolog. l. 2. c. 37.
units.tr: B. Because, since the Christians were everywhere so numerous that they filled all places, and many of them were not men of the lowest rank, they could plausibly have asserted their greater liberty by arms, had it seemed good to them. (Tertullian, Apology, bk. 2, ch. 37.)

units.la: A. Sed nonne hoc est Tyrannos animare ad eadem innocentium Subditorum?
units.tr: A. But does this not encourage tyrants to treat innocent subjects in the same way?

units.la: B. Minime: sed eos atque adeo totam Divino judicio causam permittere, nec b denegatum nobis gladium arripere: a 1 Sam. 24. 12. 2 Chron. 24. 22. b Mat. 26. 52.
units.tr: B. Not at all: rather, it leaves both the cause and the vengeance to the judgment of God, and does not take up the sword, which was not denied to us. (1 Sam. 24:12; 2 Chron. 24:22; Matt. 26:52.)

units.la: A. At multis prospere cessit adversus Principem rebellio.
units.tr: A. Yet rebellion against a prince has succeeded well for many.

units.la: B. Ad tempus fortasse, id justo permittente Deo: sed multo plures in scelerato periere auso, & li minus in hoc seculo, saltem in futuro, Prosperitas stultorum perdet eos. Pro. 1. 32.
units.tr: B. Perhaps for a time, God permitting it justly; but many more have perished who dared such wickedness, and if not in this age, at least in the future one, the prosperity of fools will destroy them. (Prov. 1:32.)

units.la: Cap. 14. De Ecclesia.
units.tr: Chapter 14. On the Church.

units.la: A Quid significat vox Ecclesiæ sensu Theologico, & maxime usitato?
units.tr: A. What does the word Ecclesia mean in the theological sense, and in its most common usage?

units.la: B. In genere cætum Christianum, sive in Christum credentium, per verbi præconium (ordinarió) & Spiritum Dei, è reliqua mundi coluvie evocatum. Act. 2. 44. 19. 2. b Ro. 10. 14. c Is. 59. 21. d Ro. 1. 7.
units.tr: B. In general, a Christian assembly, that is, of those believing in Christ, called out from the rest of the world's filth by the proclamation of the Word (ordinarily) and the Spirit of God. Acts 2. 44. 19. 2. b Ro. 10. 14. c Is. 59. 21. d Ro. 1. 7.

units.la: A. Quotuplex est Ecclesia?
units.tr: A. How many kinds of Church are there?

units.la: B. Distingui solet 1° in militantem (in Terris) & triumphantem (in cœlis;) & 2° in Visibilem & Invisibilem. 2 Cor. 10. 3, 4. Apoc. 7. 9.
units.tr: B. It is customary to distinguish, first, into militant (on earth) and triumphant (in heaven); and second, into visible and invisible. 2 Cor. 10. 3, 4. Apoc. 7. 9.

units.la: A. Unde autem oritur ista Ecclesiæ distinctio posterior?
units.tr: A. But where does this latter distinction of the Church arise from?

units.la: B. Ex varia membrorum unde componitur conditione, tum interna, tum externa.
units.tr: B. From the varied condition of the members of which it is composed, both internal and external.

units.la: A. Qui vero ex interna?
units.tr: A. What is the internal condition?

units.la: B. Nempe visibilis conflatur ex fidelibus, qui tales habentur, sive judicio charitatis, sive veritatis: invisibilis ex iis tantum qui fideles revera sunt, quorum scilicet interna indoles, etsi Deo καρδιογνώστη notissima, aciem tamen humani intellectus (nisi divinitus revelata) fugit, 1 Cor. 1, 2. Act. 8. 13. Apoc. 3. 1. Ro. 2. 29. Eph. 5. 25. Act. 9. 13. 15. Mat. 23. 28.
units.tr: B. Namely, the visible Church is made up of the faithful, who are so regarded, either by the judgment of charity or of truth; the invisible of those alone who are truly faithful, whose inner character, although most well known to God, the knower of hearts [καρδιογνώστη], escapes the sight of the human intellect (unless divinely revealed). 1 Cor. 1, 2. Act. 8. 13. Apoc. 3. 1. Ro. 2. 29. Eph. 5. 25. Act. 9. 13. 15. Mat. 23. 28.

units.la: A. Dic quomodo ab externa Ecclesiæ conditione nascitur discrimen?
units.tr: A. Explain how the distinction arises from the external condition of the Church.

units.la: B. Nimirum Visibilis dicitur Ecclesia, quæ ob multitudinem aperte profitentium veritatem, non sibi tantum ipsi, sed & hoftibusEvangelii est confpicua : Invisibilis, quæ ob membrorum five paucitatem five dispersionem ex persecutione ortam in angulis obscura, nisi sibimet ipsi, delitescit.
units.tr: B. Namely, the Church is called visible which, because of the number of those who openly profess the truth, is conspicuous not only to themselves but also to the enemies of the Gospel; the invisible is the Church which, because its members are either few or scattered, and which has arisen from persecution, lies hidden in corners, obscure except to itself.

units.la: A. Quod si Ecclesia sit unquam hoc nomine invisibilis, quomodo dicitur lux mundi? Mat. 5.
units.tr: A. But if the Church is ever invisible in this sense, how is it called the light of the world? Mat. 5.

units.la: B. Quoniam scil. in se semper lumine cœlesti perfusa, potest tamen (ut Sol ipse) aut cæcis, aut videre nolentibus aut (persecutionis & errorum) opaco interpolito collocatis minime apparere, iis interim qui filii sunt lucis utcunque radiosa.
units.tr: B. Because, namely, always bathed in heavenly light in itself, it can nevertheless (like the Sun itself) not appear at all to those who are blind, or unwilling to see, or who are placed behind the opaque interposition (of persecution and errors); meanwhile it is somewhat radiant to those who are sons of light.

units.la: A. At quomodo cum promissione Christi hoc convenit, ubi dicit, quod portæ Inferorum adversus Ecclesiam minime prævalebunt? Mat. 16.-18.
units.tr: A. But how does this agree with Christ's promise, where he says that the gates of Hell will by no means prevail against the Church? Mat. 16.-18.

units.la: B. Intelligendus est de Ecclesia Universali & Invisibili, nam de particularibus & visibilibus experientia reclamat; ut (si alia deessent testimonia) exemplo sunt Ecclesia Judaica, & 7. illæ Apocalypticæ, c. 2, & 3.
units.tr: B. It must be understood of the Universal and Invisible Church, for experience cries out against it with regard to particular and visible churches; as (if other testimonies were lacking) examples are the Jewish Church, and those seven Apocalyptic churches, c. 2 and 3.

units.la: A. An ergo non potest Ecclesia militans in terris penitus deficere?
units.tr: A. Then can the Church militant on earth not fail altogether?

units.la: B. Non potest; pugnat hoc enim cum promissionibus divinis, qualis ea est modo memorata, Mat. 16. Mat. 28. 20. Hinc seculis etiam corruptissimis, & maxime Apostaticis, ubi prorsus interiisse videretur Ecclesia, suas sibi fidelium reliquias in tuto condidisse Regem Ecclesiæ omnes docent historiae, ut 1 Reg. 19. 14, 18.
units.tr: B. It cannot; for this contradicts the divine promises of the kind just mentioned, Mat. 16. Mat. 28. 20. Hence, in even the most corrupt and especially apostate ages, when the Church seemed utterly to have perished, all histories teach that the King of the Church kept for himself remnants of the faithful in safety, as in 1 Kings 19. 14, 18.

units.la: A. Ast ubi gentium fuit Ecclesia per tot annorum centurias ante Reformantem Lutherum?
units.tr: A. But where was the Church for so many centuries before the Reformer Luther?

units.la: B. In mediis Ecclesiae hostibus captiva, oppressa saepe, variisque maculis deformata, sicut tempore Achabi Israelitica, vel ut arca Dei inter Philisthaeos ad tempus triumphata.
units.tr: B. In the midst of the Church's enemies, captive, often oppressed and disfigured by various stains, just as the Israelite Church was in the time of Ahab, or as the ark of God was for a time carried in triumph among the Philistines.

units.la: A. Qualis vero erat ista Ecclesia, quae nullibi comparuit, quae nullos sibi proprios habuit pastores, Regimen Ecclesiasticum, & disciplinam nullam, quae denique cum caetibus (quos ipsa vocat) Idololatricis communionem ordinariam exercere sustinuit? Ad ista velim ut sigillatim respondeas.
units.tr: A. What sort of Church was that which appeared nowhere, which had no pastors of its own, no ecclesiastical government, and no discipline at all, which finally was willing to keep up ordinary communion with idolatrous assemblies (as it itself calls them)? To these I would like you to reply point by point.

units.la: B. Ad primum quaesiti caput, ostensum est supra, minime necessarium esse ut Ecclesia semper compareat, nisi suis ipsius membris: at 1° ex abundanti dicimus, sub ipsa Papatus tyrannide comparuisse saepius gregem Christi, etsi obscuriorem paulo & minus frequentem, nec erubescendum est Ecclesiae, si quando grex pusillus audiat, Luc. 12. 32.) Imo nullo defuere saeculo qui veritatem Christi, idque in gravissimis fidei capitibus contra sacrilegas novitates Papicolarum, quae dictis, quae factis, quae denique proprio sanguine vindicabant. Hic Judicem appellamus Historiam Ecclesiae.
units.tr: B. To the first point of the question, it has been shown above that it is by no means necessary for the Church always to appear, except to its own members. But, first, and more than enough, we say that even under the very tyranny of the Papacy the flock of Christ has appeared fairly often, though somewhat more obscure and less numerous; nor should the Church be ashamed if at any time it hears itself called a little flock, Luke 12. 32. Indeed, in no age were lacking those who defended the truth of Christ, and that on the gravest articles of faith, against the sacrilegious novelties of the Papists; they defended it by words, by deeds, and finally by their own blood. Here we appeal to the judge, the History of the Church.

units.la: A. Quid autem de defectu Pastorum sibi peculiarium, Disciplinae, & Regiminis Ecclesiastici, sentiendum?
units.tr: A. What, then, should be thought about the lack of its own pastors, of discipline, and of ecclesiastical government?

units.la: B. Nimirum (ut alia praeteream) quod pastores illi Pontificii (quales quales) sufficerent ad tempus inserviendis Ecclesiæ commodis simpliciter necessariis, ut Scribæ & Pharisæi Ecclesiæ Judaicæ, quibus ex præceptoChristi pro tempore auscultandum erat.
units.tr: B. Namely (to pass over other things) that those Papist pastors, such as they were, would suffice for a time to serve the Church's simply necessary interests, as the scribes and Pharisees did for the Jewish Church, to whom, by Christ's precept, they had to be listened to for the time being.

units.la: A. Quid porro de isto Disciplinæ defectu statuendum?
units.tr: A. What further should be decided about this lack of discipline?

units.la: B. Disciplinam scilicet (omnibus quasi numeris absolutam) ubi haberi potest ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem apprime facere, essentiam minime constituere. a vid. 1 Cor. c. 5. &c. 11. collat. cum 1 Cor. 1. v. 2.
units.tr: B. Discipline (absolute in every respect), where it can be had, is indeed very useful for building up the Church, but it does not constitute the essence. See 1 Cor. ch. 5 etc. and 11, compared with 1 Cor. 1, v. 2.

units.la: A. Quid demum ad communionem istam cum catibus Idololatricis dicendum? potuitne ullo nomine Ecclesiæ titulum merēri, quæ se istis admiscuit?
units.tr: A. What finally must be said about that communion with idolatrous assemblies? Could a church that mixed itself with these deserve the title of Church in any sense?

units.la: B. Hoc fidelium tunc temporis infirmitatem & infortunium arguit, non prohibet quo minus (a) Ecclesiæ Universalis membra censerentur; præcipuè cum duram sub papatu servirent servitutem, nec plena Evangelii luce, ut postmodum, essent imbuti. a Apoc. 2. 13.
units.tr: B. This points to the weakness and misfortune of the faithful at that time; it does not prevent them from being counted members of the Universal Church, especially since they were serving under a harsh servitude under the papacy and had not been imbued with the full light of the Gospel, as they were afterwards. a Apoc. 2. 13.

units.la: A. Quæ sunt nota vera Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: A. What are the true marks of the Church?

units.la: B. Invisibilis eædem quæ verè fidelium, b vita scilicet verè Christiana; visibilis, sana in fundamentalibus c professio & prædicatio fidei, cum debita (quoad substantiam) administratione Sacramentorum. b 1 Jo. 2. 29. c 1 Jo. 4. 13. 14. Mat. 28. 19. 20.
units.tr: B. The marks of the invisible Church are the same as those of the truly faithful, namely a truly Christian life; the marks of the visible Church are sound profession and preaching of the faith in the fundamentals, with due administration (as to substance) of the Sacraments. b 1 Jo. 2. 29. c 1 Jo. 4. 13. 14. Mat. 28. 19. 20.

units.la: A. Nonne hæc inter notas Ecclesiæ censeri debet, quod unum in terris caput visibile agnoscat, illusque Pontificem Romanum?
units.tr: A. Should it not be counted among the marks of the Church that it acknowledges one visible head on earth, namely the Roman Pontiff?

units.la: B.
units.tr: B.

units.la: B. Nequaquam: quia nullum tale caput nobis commendat Scriptura, nedum Pont. Romanum & in talibus argumentum ex verbo Dei negativum valet.
units.tr: B. By no means: because Scripture commends no such head to us, much less the Roman Pontiff; and in such matters a negative argument from the Word of God holds.

units.la: A. Quo potissimum fundamento nititur adversa Romanensium Sententia?
units.tr: A. On what chief foundation does the opposing view of the Romanists rest?

units.la: B. Eo nimirum, quod S. Petrus tali gaudebat prae caeteris Apostolis privilegio, quod Romae sedit Episcopus, ibique Coronam tulit martyrii; demum, quod ei successor fit Pont. Rom.
units.tr: B. Namely, that St Peter enjoyed such a privilege above the other apostles, that a bishop sat at Rome and there bore the crown of martyrdom; and finally, that the Roman Pontiff is his successor.

units.la: A. Unde autem colligunt Petro indultum (prae reliquis) Episcopatum istum Oecumenicum, sive potestatem in omnia Ecclesiae militantis membra supereminentem?
units.tr: A. But how do they infer that this Oecumenical episcopate, or a power supereminent over all members of the militant Church, was granted to Peter above the rest?

units.la: B. Quod nimirum ei nominatim Christus tradidit claves Regni caelorum, atque adeo promisit super petra (quam illi Petrum ipsum interpertantur) se aedificaturum Ecclesiam suam. Mat. 16. 18. 19.
units.tr: B. Namely, because Christ expressly handed over to him the keys of the Kingdom of heaven, and so promised that he would build his Church upon the rock (which they interpret as Peter himself). Mat. 16. 18. 19.

units.la: A. Quid ad ista respondendum?
units.tr: A. What is to be answered to these things?

units.la: B. 1° Claves non uni Petro, sed omnibus Apostolis ex aequo esse concreditas liquido constat ex Mat. 18. 18. & Jo. 20. 23.
units.tr: B. First, it is clear beyond doubt that the keys were entrusted not to Peter alone but equally to all the apostles, from Mat. 18. 18. and Jo. 20. 23.

units.la: A. Cur igitur eo loci Petrum duntaxat allocutus est Christus.
units.tr: A. Why, then, did Christ address only Peter in that place?

units.la: B. Quoniam is a nomine reliquorum praeclaram illam de Christo confessionem edidit, utque ad illius nomen (respondo ad b singulos aequaliter pertinente) alluderet. a Mat. 16. 20. b Collat. cum v. 15.
units.tr: B. Because he, speaking in the name of the rest, made that famous confession about Christ, and so that he might allude to that name (which, I reply, applies equally to each of the individuals). a Mat. 16. 20. b Collat. cum v. 15.

units.la: b Collat. cum v. 15.
units.tr: b Collat. cum v. 15.

units.la: A. At primus dicitur Petrus, Mat. 10.
units.tr: A. But Peter is called "first", Mat. 10.

units.la: B. Inde ordinis fortasse colligatur primitas, nulla jurisdictionis. Primus appellatus est Petrus, quod primus omnium vocaretur à Christo; ad Apostolatum scilicet, etsi Andreas prior ad Discipulatum. confer Mat. 4. cum Jo. 1.
units.tr: B. From this perhaps a primacy of order may be gathered, but no primacy of jurisdiction. Peter was called first because he was called first of all by Christ, namely to the apostleship, although Andrew was earlier to the discipleship. Compare Mat. 4 with Jo. 1.

units.la: A. Estne aliud aliquod ex Scriptura petendum quod S. Petri in reliquos Apostolos jurisdictioni suffragetur?
units.tr: A. Is there anything else to be sought from Scripture that supports St Peter's jurisdiction over the other apostles?

units.la: B. Omnino nihil; imo nonnulla potius in speciem contraria; qualia sunt quod eum ex infirmitate carnis (statim à concesso omnibus privilegio) labentem a Satanam appellaret Christus, eique in faciem obsisteret b S. Paulus, quibus nihil simile caeteris Apostolis factum legimus, a Mat. 16. 23. b Gal. 2. 11. Adde quod Paulus asserit se nihilo inferiorem fuisse reliquis Apostolis, & consequenter non Petro, 1 Cor. 11. 5. nec ulla demum talis jurisdictionis umbra ex Scripturis ostendi poterit.
units.tr: B. Absolutely nothing; indeed there are rather some things that appear contrary, such as that Christ called him Satan when he was slipping through the weakness of the flesh (immediately after the privilege had been granted to all), and that St Paul withstood him to his face. Nothing similar is read as having been done to the other apostles. a Mat. 16. 23. b Gal. 2. 11. Add that Paul asserts he was in no way inferior to the other apostles, and consequently not to Peter, 1 Cor. 11. 5. Nor, finally, can any shadow of such jurisdiction be shown from the Scriptures.

units.la: A. Quid vero quod Ecclesiam super Petro aedificandam promisit Christus?
units.tr: A. But what about Christ's promise that he would build the Church upon Peter?

units.la: B. Non dixit super Petro, sed super hac Petra; ea nimirum fide, quam suo & reliquorum Apostolorum nomine professus est Petrus.
units.tr: B. He did not say "upon Peter," but upon this rock: that is, upon the faith which Peter professed in his own name and in that of the other Apostles.

units.la: A. Quid si demum super ipsum Petrum?
units.tr: A. What if it is upon Peter himself after all?

units.la: B. Incommodi nihil sequetur, modo 1° fundamentum statuatur Petrus, non personale (quod c solus est Christus) sed doctrinale, nec 2° doctrinale primarium, sed d secundarium, ipsi scilicet Christo Prophetae magno & super aedificantem & aedificatum; nec 3° vel hoc sensu super Petro magis, quam super{e} reliqua Prophetarum & Apostolorum Coronâ.
units.tr: B. No harm would follow, provided that (1) Peter is taken as the foundation not personally (for Christ alone is that, strictly speaking) but doctrinally; (2) not as the primary doctrinal foundation but a secondary one, namely under Christ himself, the great Prophet, who is both the builder and the one built upon; and (3) even in this sense it is not "upon Peter" any more than upon the rest of the crown of Prophets and Apostles.

units.la: A. Sed quid demum Romano Pont. in hoc negotio cum S. Petro ?
units.tr: A. But what has the Roman Pontiff to do with St Peter in this matter?

units.la: B. Non magis quàm cum Philippo aut Bartholomæo : nam potestatem istam Apostolicam (quoad eam quam ille sibi arrogat latitudinem jurisdictionis Oecumenicam) expirasse cum ipsis Apostolis (non secus) ac dona miraculorum, palam est ex historia Eccles. quæ per multas annorum à Christo Centurias tale nihil meminit, nedum agnovit.
units.tr: B. No more than with Philip or Bartholomew. For that apostolic power (as regards the "oecumenical breadth of jurisdiction" which he claims for himself) ended with the Apostles themselves, just as the gifts of miracles did. This is plain from church history, which for many centuries after Christ mentions nothing of the kind, let alone acknowledges it.

units.la: A. Quomodo igitur toto eo tempore regebatur Ecclesia ?
units.tr: A. How, then, was the Church governed during all that time?

units.la: B. In suis cujusque Parœciis (sive Diœcesibus) Episcopi independentem ab alio quovis Episcopo jurisdictionem exercebant.
units.tr: B. In their own parishes (or dioceses) the bishops exercised a jurisdiction independent of any other bishop.

units.la: A. Quod si Petrus Romæ sedem habuit Episcopalem, (idque per multos, ut ferunt, annos) nonne sequetur successoribus ejus æqualem debere statem ?
units.tr: A. But if Peter had an episcopal seat at Rome (and that for many years, as they say), must not his successors have an equal status?

units.la: B. 1° Non illis magis (data hypothesi) deberetur, quam reliquorum Apostolorum successoribus, hinc nihil Pont. accrescit Romano.
units.tr: B. (1) On the given hypothesis, it would be owed to them no more than to the successors of the other Apostles. Nothing therefore accrues to the Roman Pontiff.

units.la: 2° Non Romæ magis quam Antiochiæ, aliisque locis, ubi Petrus aliquamdiu hæsit Episcopus, deberetur.
units.tr: (2) It would be owed no more at Rome than at Antioch and the other places where Peter for some time held the episcopate.

units.la: 3° Loci successio per se nil facit ad successionem potestatis ex jure divino.
units.tr: (3) Succession to a place does nothing, in itself, for succession to power by divine right.

units.la: 4°Nec si vel maxime faceret, successione suam per tot Schismatû gravissimorû, Pontificumq; aut inindebitè electorum, aut postea haereticos manifestorum devia (ab ipsis Pontificiis abundè nobis indigitata) illæsam queant & incolumem ad S. Petri Cathedram perducere.
units.tr: (4) And even if it did, could it bring its succession safe and sound to St Peter's chair through so many grave schisms, and through pontiffs either unduly or irregularly elected, or afterwards manifestly heretical (as the Papists themselves have abundantly pointed out to us), by such crooked paths?

units.la: A. Multa tamen Ecclesia Romanæ pra reliquis hanc statuunt sedem.
units.tr: A. Yet the Church of Rome sets this see above the rest in many respects.

units.la: B. Honore quidem reverentia ut Sororem, non obsequii, ut Dominam: hoc enim fecere salvis primò suis sibi juribus, & 2° ob hanc præcipuè rationem, quod esset Romæ sedes Imperii, sicut ex antiquis Canonibus manifestum est.
units.tr: B. Indeed, by a reverence of honour, as a sister, not by obedience, as a mistress. They did this, first, saving their own rights; and second, chiefly for this reason, that Rome was the seat of the empire, as is clear from the ancient canons.

units.la: A. Verum suis sibi res habente Romano Pont. nunquid alienum est à mente Christi, ut Presbyterus reliquus in unaquaque Diœcesi unus superemineat & præsit Episcopus?
units.tr: A. But is it contrary to the mind of Christ, in the case of the Roman Pontiff's own see, that among the presbyters in each diocese one should stand out and preside as bishop?

units.la: B. Nequaquam, nam primò in ipsis Apostolorum temporibus talis reperitur Episcopatus, ut in Epist. ad Tim. & Tit. & in Angelis istis 7. Eccles. Apocalypticis, ad quos ut Antistites, per S. Johan. literas dat ipse Christus monitorias. Et 2° à die[?] Apostolorum ætate ad avorum usque nostrorum tempora nulla unquam in Terris audita est fine Episcopo Ecclesia Christiana, ni omnes sal'ant historiæ.
units.tr: B. By no means. For first, in the very times of the Apostles such an episcopate is found, as in the Epistles to Timothy and Titus and in the seven angels of the churches in the Apocalypse, to whom Christ himself, through St John, sends admonitory letters as to chief pastors. And second, from the age of the Apostles down to the times of our grandparents, no Christian Church on earth was ever heard of without a bishop, unless all histories lie.

units.la: A. Sed à facto ad jus non valet argumentum?
units.tr: A. But an argument from fact to right is not valid?

units.la: B. Imo hoc in caiu plurimum; nam indigna est vigilantissima Christi super Ecclesia sua solicitudine cogitatio, ut eam ab illius usque incunabulis ad caniciem fere finxeret tali politia uti, quam ipse minus probaret.
units.tr: B. On the contrary, in this case it is very valid. For it is unworthy to think that Christ, in his most watchful care for his Church, would have let it be shaped from its very cradle almost to grey hairs by a polity which he himself would not approve.

units.la: A. Quam statuis Ecclesiastica potestatis in sibi subditos materiam?
units.tr: A. What are the matters over which ecclesiastical power is exercised over its subjects?

units.la: B. Ea duplex est, aut scilicet res in se adiaphora, aut in lege Dei comprehensa.
units.tr: B. It is twofold: either things in themselves indifferent (adiaphora), or things contained in the law of God.

units.la: A. An circa utramque modo consimili occupatur?
units.tr: A. Is it exercised over both in the same way?

units.la: B. Nequaquam; habet enim Ecclesia potestatem in materiâ adiaphora νομοθετικὴν (sive leges condendi) Christo subordinatam, ad ædificationem gregis Dominici. e 1 Cor. 14. 26.
units.tr: B. Not at all. For the Church has legislative power [νομοθετικὴν] (that is, the power to make laws) over indifferent matters, subordinate to Christ, for the edification of the Lord's flock. 1 Cor. 14. 26.

units.la: A. Id unde constat?
units.tr: A. How do you know this?

units.la: B. Partim ex verbo Dei, partim ex ufitatissima veterum Ecclesiarum praxi, simulac à persecutionum æstu satis respiraverant. f 1 Cor. 14.40.
units.tr: B. Partly from the word of God, and partly from the very common practice of the ancient churches, as soon as they had recovered somewhat from the heat of persecution. 1 Cor. 14. 40.

units.la: A. In rebus lege morali divina, aut jam præceptis aut prohibitis, quomodo ista exercetur Ecclesia potestas?
units.tr: A. In matters of the divine moral law, whether commanded or forbidden, how is the Church's power exercised?

units.la: B. Non ut quicquam f immutet, sed ut omnia suis quoq; sanctionibusg corroboret: alioqui parendum est Deo magis quam hominibus, Act. 4. 18 19. f Deut. 4.2. Gal. 1.8.9.12. g1 Cor. 5. ad v. 6. Judæ 22.23.
units.tr: B. Not so as to change anything, but so as to strengthen everything with its own sanctions as well; otherwise "we must obey God rather than men," Acts 4. 18, 19. Deut. 4. 2. Gal. 1. 8, 9, 12. 1 Cor. 5. at v. 6. Jude 22, 23.

units.la: A. In controversiis fidei quænam sunt partes Ecclesiæ?
units.tr: A. In controversies of faith, what are the duties of the Church?

units.la: B. Se Fidei h Testem, i Custodem, k Interpretem, (idque non nisi secundum 1 Analogiam fidei) præstare, m seductos in viam placidè revocare, in n seductores & præfractos gravius animadvertere, h Act. 1. 8. 1 Tim. 3.15. i Judæ 3. 1 Tim. 1.11. k Job. 33.23. Act. 15. ad v.30. 1 Rom. 12.6. vid. Eccles.Angl. Art. 20. m 2 Tim. 2. 24.25. n Tit. 1. 10, 11.13.
units.tr: B. To act as witness of the faith, its guardian and its interpreter (and this only according to the analogy of faith); to gently call back those who have gone astray onto the way, and to deal more severely with the seducers and the obstinate. Acts 1. 8. 1 Tim. 3. 15. Jude 3. 1 Tim. 1. 11. Job 33. 23. Acts 15. at v. 30. Rom. 12. 6. See the Anglican Articles, Art. 20. 2 Tim. 2. 24, 25. Tit. 1. 10, 11, 13.

units.la: A.
units.tr: A.

units.la: A. Estne vero Ecclesia Interpres infallibilis?
units.tr: A. Is the Church's interpretation of Scripture infallible?

units.la: B. Reverenter o auscultandum est Ecclesiæ, imo & in illius sententiâ (ubi, nil verbo Dei ad‑ versum statuitur) eousque humiliter acquie‑ scendum, ut ne illius voci palam contra obltre‑ pamus, nec paci quoquo modo aut damnum aut molestiam inferre velimus. Arg. à minori vid. oMat.23.3. & Eccles.Angl. Art. 21.
units.tr: B. The Church is to be heard with reverence; indeed, in its judgment (where nothing is laid down contrary to the Word of God) we must acquiesce so humbly that we do not openly oppose its voice, nor wish in any way to bring loss or trouble upon its peace. Argument from the lesser. See Matt. 23. 3, and the Anglican Articles, Art. 21.

units.la: A. Sed nisi tum Interpres, tum Judex in Terris detur infallibilis, quis erit in Ecclesia finis controversiarum?
units.tr: A. But unless an interpreter and a judge on earth is given as infallible, who will bring an end to controversies in the Church?

units.la: B. Resp. 1o. Non expectandum esse finem omnium circa-religionem controversiarum, dum Ecclesia versatur in via, præmonentibus in contrarium & oChristo & p Apost. suffragante itidem universa Ecclesiæ historiâ. oMat.18. 7. p 1 Cor.11. 19.
units.tr: B. Answer: (1) One must not expect an end to all controversies about religion while the Church is still on its way, Christ forewarning us to the contrary, and the whole history of the Church, with the Apostle lending his support, bearing witness likewise. Matt. 18. 7. 1 Cor. 11. 19.

units.la: 2. Ad nullum talem Judicem in rebus fidei relegavit Christianos aut S. Scr. aut Ecclesia Primitiva, in qua tamen subinde gliscebant schismata & discordiæ.
units.tr: (2) Neither Holy Scripture nor the primitive Church referred Christians, in matters of faith, to any such infallible judge; yet schisms and discords from time to time flared up in that Church.

units.la: 3. Sine Judice hoc in Terris infallibili Ecclesiam & consistere posse & vigere, testem provocamus experientiam, cum per annos à Christo incarnato 300. & amplius, nulla esset in Concilio generali Ecclesia repræsentativa, nedum Ecclesia virtualis (ut vocant) habitus est Pont.Romanus; tota autem credentium multitudo sententiam latura in unum aliquem locum convenire non potuit.
units.tr: (3) That the Church can both subsist and flourish without such an infallible judge on earth, we call experience as our witness. For through the 300 and more years since Christ was incarnate there was no representative Church in a general council, let alone a "virtual" Church (as they call it) held to be the Roman Pontiff; and the whole multitude of believers could not come together in one place to pronounce judgment.

units.la: 4. Nec qui Judicem hunc falso venditant Pontificii, aut quis sit, inter se unquam convenerunt, aut quemcunque demum statuant, objecti nobis mali remedium inveniunt A.
units.tr: (4) Nor have the Papists, who falsely peddle this judge, ever agreed among themselves on who he is; and whoever they set up, they find no remedy for the evil objected to us.

units.la: A. Quorsum itaque indies audiuntur Pastores Ecclesiæ, fi non sint infallibiles?
units.tr: A. Why, then, are the ministers of the Church heard daily, if they are not infallible?

units.la: B. Non id à bono Pastore requiritur, ut non possit, sed utq nolit fallere, tenentur autem populi eos reverenter r audire, ut ad examen vocatis quæ Christi nomine dicunt omnibus, quod bonum est ampleЯantur & retineant. q2Cor. 4.2. r1Tim. 4.13,15. Mal.2. Act.17.11. 1Thef.5 21. 1Cor. 10.15.
units.tr: B. It is not required of a good minister that he be unable to err, but that he be unwilling to deceive. The people are bound to hear them reverently, so that, called to the test, they may embrace and hold fast what they say in Christ's name, "that which is good." 2 Cor. 4. 2. 1 Tim. 4. 13, 15. Mal. 2. Acts 17. 11. 1 Thess. 5. 21. 1 Cor. 10. 15.

units.la: Cap. 15. De Sacramentis.
units.tr: Chap. 15. Of the Sacraments.

units.la: A. QUid proprie est Sacramentum novi Fœderis?
units.tr: A. What properly is a sacrament of the New Covenant?

units.la: B. Est {f}signum & sigillum externum Justitiæ quæ est per fidem,{t} diviuitus institutum. {f} Rom.4. 11. Exod. 12.13. Col.2. 12. Tit.3.5. 1 Cor.10.16. {t} Mat.28. 20. 1 Cor.11.23.
units.tr: B. It is an external {f}sign and seal of the righteousness which is by faith, {t}divinely instituted. {f} Rom.4. 11. Exod. 12.13. Col.2. 12. Tit.3.5. 1 Cor.10.16. {t} Mat.28. 20. 1 Cor.11.23.

units.la: A. Quotuplicia sunt ejusmodi Sacramenta?
units.tr: A. How many kinds of such sacraments are there?

units.la: B. Duplicia; alia sub lege, sive Judaica, Circumcisio nimirum, & Agnus Paschalis; alia sub Evangelio, sive Christiana, Baptismus, & Cœna Domini. De prioribus vid. Gen. 17. & Exod. 12.
units.tr: B. There are two kinds: some under the law, that is, Jewish, namely circumcision and the Passover lamb; others under the Gospel, that is, Christian, baptism and the Lord's Supper. On the former see Gen. 17. and Exod. 12.

units.la: A. Utriusque generis Sacramenta quomodo distinguuntur?
units.tr: A. How are the sacraments of each kind distinguished?

units.la: B. Est alterum scilicet initians, idque tam infantium quam Adultorum, Circumcisio & Baptismus; alterum continuans & confirmans, idq; tantum Adultorum, Agnus Pasc. & Cœna Domini.
units.tr: B. One kind is initiating, and this applies to infants as well as adults: circumcision and baptism. The other is continuing and confirming, and applies only to adults: the Passover lamb and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: A. Unde liquet Circumcisionem & Bapt. fuisse Sacramenta initiatoria?
units.tr: A. How is it clear that circumcision and baptism were initiatory sacraments?

units.la: B. Ex eo, quod in Ecclesiam Judaicam {u} mas omnis per circumcisionē solenniter admitteretur; in Christianam, (sive mas, sive fœmina) excipitur nemo nisi per {x} Baptismum. Proin utrumvis femel duntaxat adhibitum legimus, non autem, ut Sacramenta Confirmantia, sæpius repetendum. {u} Gen. 17.10.12. {x} Mat. 28. 19.
units.tr: B. From the fact that in the Jewish Church every {u} male was solemnly admitted by circumcision; in the Christian Church no one, whether male or female, is received except by {x} baptism. Hence we read that each of these was applied only once, and not, like the confirming sacraments, repeated again and again. {u} Gen. 17.10.12. {x} Mat. 28. 19.

units.la: A. Quid de aliis 5. Sacramentis Pontificiis censendum? A
units.tr: A. What is to be thought of the other five Papist sacraments?

units.la: {f} sigillum ... [marginal reference marks as printed in the text]
units.tr: {f} seal ...

units.la: B. Eorum nulla esse proprie Sacramenta, hoc est sensu quo Baptismus & Coena Domini in confesso sunt habenda.
units.tr: B. None of them is properly a sacrament, that is, in the sense in which baptism and the Lord's Supper are acknowledged to be sacraments.

units.la: A. Ostende discrimen?
units.tr: A. Show the difference.

units.la: B. Omnium generale idque palmarium hoc est, quod nullibi pro Sacramentis à Christo (ad quem unum utrisque consentientibus id negotii pertinet) instituta legimus. At de Baptismo, & Cæna Domini, lis nulla movetur.
units.tr: B. The general difference, and the chief one, is this: nowhere do we read that these were instituted as sacraments by Christ, to whom alone, as both sides agree, this business belongs. But there is no dispute about baptism and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: A. Quid ad ista in specie dicendum, & 1. de Ordine, seu Ordinatione Ministrorum Evangelii?
units.tr: A. What is to be said of these in particular, and 1. of Order, or Ordination of the Ministers of the Gospel?

units.la: B. Non esse Sacramentum sensu quo diximus; 1° Quod nullam (sicut Baptismus, & Coena Domini, Circumcisio & Agn. Pasc.) externam habeat & aspectabilem materiam; 2° quod ad certum hominum genus restringatur, non autem (ut ista) ad omnes ex æquo Christianos pertineat. y 1 Cor. 12. 17.
units.tr: B.
